Abstract: Time-dependent tidal interactions during the late inspiral of binary neutron stars encode valuable information about neutron-star structure, but systematically extending the familiar Newtonian mode-sum picture into full general relativity is nontrivial. In this paper, we develop a practical relativistic implementation of mode-sum tidal response for non-rotating neutron stars in Regge-Wheeler gauge. Using near-zone boundary conditions, we systematically define the interior tidal field, the relativistic overlap integrals, and the corresponding mode amplitudes. The good is that the dominant f-mode contribution is remarkably robust, reproducing the direct matching calculation to within $\sim 3$\% across the equations of state we consider. The bad is that the operator governing mode inner product is not positive definite on the full Regge-Wheeler-gauge function space, so the relativistic mode sum truncated at ${\cal{O}}(\omega^2)$ is not expected to strictly converge to the direct matching solution. The subtle is that the tidal field inside the star is not unique, although this ambiguity has only a limited impact on the dominant f-mode response for the classes of extensions studied here. Our results establish the practical utility of relativistic mode-sum approximations, while making clear that their predictive power comes from a controlled low-mode description, rather than from a formally convergent strong-field expansion.

arxiv.org/abs/2606.19757.title: Graviton Floor
arxiv.org/abs/2606.19757.excerpt:
arXiv:2606.19757v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: It has been observed that the Universe is permeated by the cosmic photon background, ranging from radio waves to gamma rays. We investigate the conversion of the photon background into gravitons in the presence of background magnetic fields in the Milky Way Galaxy and in blazar jets. We find that the resulting graviton background is dominated by the contribution generated in blazar jets. Importantly, this graviton background constitutes a graviton floor for high-frequency gravitational wave detectors searching for new physics, analogous to the neutrino floor.

arxiv.org/abs/2608.07172.title: New Universal Relations for Magnetized Neutron Stars
arxiv.org/abs/2608.07172.excerpt:
arXiv:2608.07172v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Unlike the neutron-star mass--radius relation, which depends sensitively on the internal stellar structure through the equation of state of dense nuclear matter, certain neutron-star properties obey approximately universal relations that exhibit only weak dependence on the equation of state. In this paper, we explore new universal relations for magnetized neutron stars. We focus on a purely poloidal dipolar magnetic-field configuration and treat the effects of the magnetic field perturbatively to second order in the field strength. After appropriately normalizing the relevant quantities by the stellar mass and the magnetic-field strength at the pole, we first identify an exact universal relation between the magnetic dipole moment and stellar compactness. We then find approximate universal relations among the magnetic dipole moment, magnetically-induced stellar quadrupole moment, and ellipticity, with fractional variations due to the equation of state at the level of O(10%). We support these numerical findings with analytic estimates for Newtonian polytropes, which reproduce the observed behavior. Among the newly discovered relations, the one connecting the magnetic dipole moment and stellar quadrupole moment may be particularly useful for the analysis of gravitational-wave signals from binaries containing magnetized neutron stars.

arxiv.org/abs/2608.10264.title: On the nature of oscillating modes of proto-neutron stars
arxiv.org/abs/2608.10264.excerpt:
arXiv:2608.10264v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Newborn proto-neutron stars (PNS) are potential targets of gravitational wave asteroseismology, the study of the (inner) structure of stars via their oscillation modes. To prepare for the eventual detection of such modes by current and future gravitational wave observatories, theoretical studies have obtained the possible spectrum of oscillations. However, there has been disagreement when it comes to identifying and classifying specific modes according to the physical mechanism that excites them. In this paper, we present a novel scheme to classify the oscillation modes of a newly born PNS surrounded by a stalled accretion shock in core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe). Our classification is physically motivated, as it is based on the energy of the restoring forces of the mode. We investigate the nature of the modes by considering the different regions of the CCSN that they stem from. We apply this scheme to a set of 28 non-rotating 1D, 2D and 3D CCSN simulations performed with two different numerical codes and using different progenitors and equations of state. In that way, we find that there are different families of f-, p- and g-modes in the system, living in different areas. More specifically, we identify two families of f- and p-modes associated with the PNS and the shock, respectively, and two families of g-modes originating from the two convectively stable regions, one in the PNS core and one near its surface. We also find that the dominant high-frequency emission mode is the f-mode of the PNS, associated with the strong density gradient at its surface. Our classification procedure is automatic, performs consistently for all the models considered, and paves the way to systematic studies of the dependence of the mode frequencies on the PNS properties, with direct application to parameter estimation from future observations of gravitational wave signals.

arxiv.org/abs/2609.28953.title: Constraining the Quadratic-mode Amplitude Coupling in GW250114
arxiv.org/abs/2609.28953.excerpt:
arXiv:2609.28953v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Detecting quadratic quasi-normal modes in black hole ringdowns would provide evidence for nonlinear gravitational dynamics, while measuring their properties would enable tests of the corresponding predictions of general relativity. Specifically, second-order black hole perturbation theory predicts that their amplitudes scale with the product of the amplitudes of their parent linear modes, with a coupling coefficient that depends on the spin of the remnant black hole. This mode-specific coupling coefficient has not yet been directly measured from gravitational wave data. Here, we use Bayesian inference on the GW250114 ringdown, modeled with the $220$, $221$, and $220\times220$ modes, to infer the amplitude-coupling coefficient of the $220\times220$ mode. The inferred coefficient is consistent with predictions from numerical relativity fits and second-order perturbation theory; no comparison shows a deviation exceeding $1.3 \sigma$. Although the current data cannot distinguish among these spin-dependent predictions, this measurement establishes a basis for more stringent observational tests of nonlinear gravitational dynamics in black-hole ringdowns.

arxiv.org/abs/2610.20772.title: Optimal Strategies for Gravitational-Wave Memory Detection with Noise Marginalization in Pulsar Timing Arrays
arxiv.org/abs/2610.20772.excerpt:
arXiv:2610.20772v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Current pulsar timing arrays could detect gravitational wave memory, which would provide a unique test of general relativity. In order to optimize our searches for gravitational wave memory in pulsar timing arrays, we integrate the optimal frequentist statistics for GW memory into the \texttt{enterprise} code suite. We additionally test a noise marginalized version of this statistic, and compare it's effectiveness to the simpler maximum posterior method. We perform these tests on simulated pulsar timing array with red and white noise content, as well as the NANOGrav $15$-year data set. We find no significant variations in our detection statistics between the noise-marginalized and the maximum-posterior methods for the simulated datasets, and only small variations in the NANOGrav $15$-year comparisons. We conclude that for realistic PTAs the noise-marginalization method could be useful for assigning a false alarm probability to Bayesian results, though the maximum posterior method is sufficient for identifying potentially detectable signals.

arxiv.org/abs/2610.29941.title: Rotation slows the instability of Ellis-Bronnikov wormholes
arxiv.org/abs/2610.29941.excerpt:
arXiv:2610.29941v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Rotation weakens the radial instability of Ellis-Bronnikov wormholes in slow-rotation perturbation theory. We investigate its nonlinear effect by evolving stationary rotating drainholes supported by a phantom scalar field. We construct the backgrounds with an independent spectral solver, validate them against published symmetric solutions, and identify a misprint in a published field equation that did not affect the original authors' numerical results. Evolutions perturbed only by discretization error show that rotation slows the collapse. At intermediate spins some throats expand, with the direction of departure depending on the effective perturbation. At the fastest evolved spin, the throat's areal radius shows no growing departure through evolution time $t=150$ in code units, about 28 e-folding times of the static instability, at three resolutions. Two other rapidly rotating models also show no growth over their reliable evolution intervals. Collapsing rotating throats emit an axisymmetric quadrupolar gravitational-wave burst whose energy increases between the two spins compared. Second-order initial data excite the instability through their background truncation error. The results establish slower collapse and prolonged absence of detected radial growth for the sampled asymmetric backgrounds, over finite times from initially axisymmetric data.

arxiv.org/abs/2611.00918.title: Sensitivity of the IceCube atmospheric muon rate to decadal trends in the effective atmospheric temperature
arxiv.org/abs/2611.00918.excerpt:
arXiv:2611.00918v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Decadal changes in the Antarctic stratosphere, generally associated with ozone recovery and shifts in polar circulation, are of broad geophysical interest. However, independent long-term measurements of the atmosphere above the Antarctic interior are scarce. We assess whether the atmospheric muon rate recorded by IceCube could constrain decadal changes in the effective atmospheric temperature, $T_\mathrm{eff}$, a weighted average of temperature through the atmosphere that is most sensitive to the stratosphere. Using public atmospheric reanalysis data and records of cosmic-ray, solar, and geomagnetic variability, we reproduce the measured seasonal response of the IceCube muon rate. We then test whether the same response applies to long-term temperature changes with a different vertical temperature profile. The limiting requirement is detector stability rather than counting statistics: an unmodeled muon rate drift of $1\%\,\mathrm{decade^{-1}}$ would mimic a temperature trend of $2.8\,\mathrm{K\,decade^{-1}}$. The long-term rate must therefore be stable to approximately $0.3\%\,\mathrm{decade^{-1}}$. Within this budget, snow accumulation contributions can be constrained. For a 14-year record, atmospheric variability gives a one-sided 95% CL statistical sensitivity of $1.6\,\mathrm{K\,decade^{-1}}$. Given this sensitivity, the $\sim0.9,\mathrm{K,decade^{-1}}$ cooling indicated by the 2011-2025 atmospheric records would be constrained at the 95% confidence level after approximately 22 years of measurement.

newscientist.com/article/2598085-cold-th.excerpt: Many are convinced that ice baths or cold showers are an effective way to speed recovery after exercise, but a study finds that cold therapy may actually have the opposite effect

newscientist.com/article/2598048-a-true-.excerpt: When we talk about prehistoric foods, we often focus on meat or perhaps cereal grains. But columnist Michael Marshall finds that ancient humans may have dined on more insects than we previously thought

newscientist.com/article/2597990-prehist.excerpt: Unusually large handaxes weighing up to 3 kilograms have puzzled archaeologists because they are so unwieldy, but their function may have been purely symbolic

newscientist.com/article/2597812-weird-u.excerpt: An experiment with ultracold potassium atoms has revealed details of a type of turbulence that only exists in the quantum realm and relies on odd tangles of stringy whirlpools

quantamagazine.org/did-life-begin-in-an-.title: Did Life Begin in an RNA World?
quantamagazine.org/did-life-begin-in-an-.excerpt: Some believe the earliest life emerged from self-copying molecules that could mutate and even evolve. But that may not have been enough. The post Did Life Begin in an RNA World? first appeared on Quanta Magazine

phys.org/news/2026-11-math-anxiety-stude.excerpt: Artificial intelligence is increasingly becoming part of everyday life and work. AI can generate information, summarize evidence and perform calculations. However, it does not remove the need for critical thinking and conceptual understanding.

phys.org/news/2026-11-pulse-pairs-reveal.title: Light-pulse pairs reveal the femtosecond decay of an inner-shell hole in xenon atoms
phys.org/news/2026-11-pulse-pairs-reveal.excerpt: Researchers at the UVSOR Synchrotron Facility (Institute for Molecular Science, Japan) and partner institutions have observed the decay of a xenon 4d core hole, an inner-shell vacancy, directly in the time domain. They used pairs of phase-coherent extreme ultraviolet pulses from a synchrotron to make the photoelectron wave packets they released interfere. The contrast of the interference fringes decreased over a few femtoseconds as the delay between the pulses increased. A model using literature core-hole lifetimes of about 6 femtoseconds reproduced this rapid decay of the fringe contrast. The study is published in the journal Physical Review A.

phys.org/news/2026-11-ai-atomic-reveal-s.title: AI-assisted atomic models reveal how protective shells regulate aluminum nanoparticle oxidation
phys.org/news/2026-11-ai-atomic-reveal-s.excerpt: Building an accurate model of how atoms interact is a complicated process. Researchers must choose new calculations, test successive models and track the mechanisms behind each interaction. But a newly developed AI agent called MLP Copilot has made this process much easier by bridging computational tools and scientific evidence with human supervision.

phys.org/news/2026-11-barium-titanate-op.title: Barium titanate's optical properties emerge more clearly after decades of widely varying measurements
phys.org/news/2026-11-barium-titanate-op.excerpt: A KAIST-led research team has characterized how light propagates through and is absorbed by barium titanate (BTO), a promising material for next-generation optical communication devices. By clarifying optical properties that had been difficult to determine because of the material's complex internal structure, the study provides a foundation for designing these devices.

phys.org/news/2026-11-electrical-techniq.title: Electrical technique concentrates milk without using heat, challenging traditional preservation methods
phys.org/news/2026-11-electrical-techniq.excerpt: Dehydrating milk to turn it into powder is, today, an energy-intensive process that subjects the product to high temperatures. Powdered milk is widely used by the food industry and allows the product to be stored and transported in a stable condition for long periods of time without the need for refrigeration. While industrial methods are effective, they have high energy costs and can alter heat-sensitive components, such as whey proteins, enzymes or vitamins.

phys.org/news/2026-11-fossil-emissions-d.title: Fossil CO₂ emissions projected to decrease in 2026 amid clean energy growth and Iran conflict
phys.org/news/2026-11-fossil-emissions-d.excerpt: Global carbon emissions from fossil fuels are projected to decrease by 0.4% in 2026—driven by expansion of solar and wind power and the Iran conflict—according to new research by the Global Carbon Project. The 2026 edition (the 21st annual report) is published in the journal Earth System Science Data.

phys.org/news/2026-11-power-strangers.ht.excerpt: You're walking through the farmers market with a screaming toddler tucked under your arm football style. You're tired, you're leaving without the produce you came for and you're embarrassed.

phys.org/news/2026-11-gatineau-foliage-r.title: Gatineau Park foliage reveals local Cold War nuclear testing legacy
phys.org/news/2026-11-gatineau-foliage-r.excerpt: For more than six decades, local scientists have collected sugar maple leaves from Gatineau Park to measure their radiocarbon levels, creating the longest continuous record of its kind. Now, a study of those leaves led by the André E. Lalonde National Facility for Accelerator Mass Spectrometry (AEL-AMS) located at the University of Ottawa shows that the effects of Cold War–era nuclear weapons testing have only recently disappeared from the local biosphere. The study, titled "Stored carbohydrates buffer Bomb and Suess radiocarbon effects in maple leaves across a 65-year Ottawa region record," was published in Scientific Reports.

phys.org/news/2026-11-accidental-discove.title: Accidental discovery enables room-temperature recrystallization of molybdenum
phys.org/news/2026-11-accidental-discove.excerpt: Researchers at the University of Rochester and Technion–Israel Institute of Technology accidentally discovered a new way to rearrange the internal structure of molybdenum—an extremely heat-resistant metal—at room temperature. Molybdenum is typically used to reinforce nuclear reactors, jet engine turbine blades and rocket nozzles because it doesn't melt until it is heated to more than 2,600°C (4,712°F). Controlling its atomic structure at room temperature could open the door to more applications, including next-generation semiconductors.

phys.org/news/2026-11-amino-acid-andes-v.title: Study identifies single amino acid change that alters Andes virus protein behavior in human cells
phys.org/news/2026-11-amino-acid-andes-v.excerpt: Mount Sinai researchers have identified a single amino acid difference between rodent- and human-derived Andes virus isolates that changes how a key viral protein behaves inside human cells. The findings help explain biological differences between closely related virus isolates.

phys.org/news/2026-11-starling-declining.title: Starling numbers are declining—we're investigating whether their spectacular murmuration displays are changing too
phys.org/news/2026-11-starling-declining.excerpt: Every autumn, from city centers to wetlands, starling murmurations attract crowds of spectators. Thousands of birds fill the sky, twisting and turning in extraordinary waves as the sun sets. An entire flock moves as one, creating shapes that shift and dissolve as quickly as they appear.

phys.org/news/2026-11-methane-microbes-g.title: Methane-eating microbes grown on electrodes build electrically conductive nanowires
phys.org/news/2026-11-methane-microbes-g.excerpt: Certain microorganisms (anaerobic methanotrophic archaea, or ANME) consume methane and convert it into electricity, as research conducted four years ago by microbiologist Cornelia Welte of Radboud University revealed. New research by Welte and her colleagues published in Nature Communications now shows that these methane-consuming organisms do this by producing nanowires through which they can transmit the electricity they generate. The researchers have also succeeded in cultivating these specific microorganisms in almost pure form in the lab.

phys.org/news/2026-11-el-nio-polycrisis-.title: El Niño 2026–27 as a polycrisis: What happens when health and energy systems fail simultaneously?
phys.org/news/2026-11-el-nio-polycrisis-.excerpt: Open any news feed from the past few months, and the disasters arrive in a stream: smoke reaching dangerous levels throughout Canada and flash floods in Ottawa, Montréal and Toronto; heat and drought arriving together on every continent.

phys.org/news/2026-11-play-critical-role.title: Water may play critical role in how our tissues stretch and spring back
phys.org/news/2026-11-play-critical-role.excerpt: Every time your heart beats, your lungs expand, or your skin stretches, a remarkable protein called elastin helps your body return to its original shape. But what exactly gives this protein its elasticity? For more than 50 years, scientists have debated whether elastin's ability to stretch and recoil comes primarily from the protein's own flexibility or from its interactions with surrounding water molecules.

phys.org/news/2026-11-archaeological-iri.title: Archaeological finds at an Irish fort reveal insights into the finer side of medieval life
phys.org/news/2026-11-archaeological-iri.excerpt: Popular media, from computer games to movies, often portray medieval life as being dominated by fighters and farmers. In these depictions, there's little evidence of a world beyond political struggle and simple subsistence.

phys.org/news/2026-11-endangered-leather.excerpt: A hopeful story for the world's largest, critically endangered sea turtle may be playing out along the sandy beaches of Ecuador.

phys.org/news/2026-11-machine-reveals-fi.title: Machine learning reveals how often fish schooling evolved—and repeatedly disappeared
phys.org/news/2026-11-machine-reveals-fi.excerpt: Scientists have used new machine learning techniques to investigate a topic no one has ever found a way to study: the evolution of fish moving together in schools across thousands of species. The new paper, published Nov. 6 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, is among the largest studies of the evolution of any behavior ever conducted in any group of species, according to the authors. The research shows that behaviors, which have previously been difficult to quantify, can be studied at a large evolutionary scale.

phys.org/news/2026-11-tin-deposits-sourc.title: Tin deposits are formed from source rocks, not cooling
phys.org/news/2026-11-tin-deposits-sourc.excerpt: New research from the University of St Andrews has uncovered the primary drivers of tin mineralization, which will have significant implications for the discovery of tin deposits critical to the energy transition.

phys.org/news/2026-11-parasite-linked-ca.excerpt: A parasitic infection commonly associated with cats may be associated with severe, potentially sight-threatening ocular disease in dogs, according to a new study by researchers at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

phys.org/news/2026-11-tree-rich-landscap.excerpt: Tropical farmers are often expected to choose between high crop yields and protecting wildlife. However, an international team of researchers led by the University of Vienna, in collaboration with the universities of Göttingen and Würzburg in Germany and Bioversity International in Peru, shows that biodiversity conservation reinforces cacao production in agroforests via associated ecosystem services, such as natural pest control. The new study, published in Communications Earth & Environment, provides important evidence for sustainable farm and landscape management in one of the world's most biodiverse regions.

phys.org/news/2026-11-elt-probe-ultra-di.excerpt: We've been waiting a long time for the Extremely Large Telescope's first light, scheduled for March 2029. Telescopes this large, powerful and costly always have multiple science goals, and that's true for the ELT. One of its science goals is to study fundamental aspects of the universe, including dark matter.

phys.org/news/2026-11-early-humans-keeps.excerpt: Most of us are familiar with the urge to pick up a seashell from the beach or keep a stone from a hiking trip. The object itself may be ordinary, but to the person who keeps it, it serves as a reminder of a particular moment, place or person. Where did this behavior come from? Did early humans do the same? A new study by Tel Aviv University researchers suggests that this practice stretches back approximately half a million years, with important consequences for the evolution of memory.

universetoday.com/articles/tiny-solar-wh.title: Tiny Solar Whirlpools May Hold the Secret to the Sun’s Blistering Corona
universetoday.com/articles/tiny-solar-wh.excerpt: For the second time in a few weeks, we’re writing about research into the temperature gap between the Sun’s surface and its corona. More and more data from various missions continue to feed this wave of discovery. A new paper by Katariina Nykyri of Embry-Riddle, recently published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, adds to this growing body of work. She argues that millions of tiny whirlpools scattered across the Sun’s surface could be the energetic engine driving that temperature difference.

earthsky.org/space/lava-planets-surprisi.title: Atmosphere of lava planet: ‘A cloudy, reflective sunscreen’
earthsky.org/space/lava-planets-surprisi.excerpt: New observations of super-Earth TOI-561 b by the Webb telescope show again that the atmosphere of lava planet TOI-561 b does exist, and is very reflective. The post Atmosphere of lava planet: ‘A cloudy, reflective sunscreen’ first appeared on EarthSky .

earthsky.org/tonight/summer-triangle-in-.title: See the Summer Triangle in the northern autumn sky
earthsky.org/tonight/summer-triangle-in-.excerpt: Look west in the evening to see the Summer Triangle in autumn. Its 3 bright stars - Vega, Deneb and Altair - are in 3 different constellations. The post See the Summer Triangle in the northern autumn sky first appeared on EarthSky .

nature.com/articles/d41586-026-03620-z.title: Metascience should be a source of evidence, not a means of control
nature.com/articles/d41586-026-03620-z.excerpt: Nature, Published online: 10 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03620-z The field has captured the interest of politicians. There are positives — but governments must not misuse the data.

newscientist.com/article/2598161-correct.title: Correcting quantum computer errors may be more complicated than expected
newscientist.com/article/2598161-correct.excerpt: Correcting quantum computer errors is key for making the devices practical, but some types of errors, and the complications they could introduce, may be more likely to occur than we had thought

phys.org/news/2026-11-cosmic-environment.title: How the cosmic environment depletes galaxies of their gas
phys.org/news/2026-11-cosmic-environment.excerpt: An international team of researchers, led by Jonathan Freundlich (University of Strasbourg, Astronomical Observatory), has revealed how a dense cosmic environment depletes galaxies of their gas. By mapping the molecular gas in a galaxy group located 7 billion light-years away, they found that the galaxies in this group harbor, on average, gas reservoirs reduced by more than half compared to similar isolated galaxies. The results of this study are published in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.

phys.org/news/2026-11-antarctic-analysis.title: Antarctic water analysis reveals unexpected stability in dissolved organic carbon
phys.org/news/2026-11-antarctic-analysis.excerpt: Researchers have analyzed water samples collected during two expeditions aboard the research icebreaker Polarstern to investigate how life and changing conditions on the Antarctic continental shelf affect carbon carried into the deep ocean. Published in Nature Communications, the study reveals a surprising finding: Despite intense biological activity and major changes in the water masses, the amount and make-up of dissolved organic matter remain almost unchanged.

phys.org/news/2026-11-walmart-nearby.htm.title: When a Walmart closes, what happens to nearby stores?
phys.org/news/2026-11-walmart-nearby.htm.excerpt: Shoppers often greet the closure of a Walmart with dismay, while competitors find cause to celebrate.

phys.org/news/2026-11-scientists-magneti.title: Scientists discover new way to control magnetic waves for future quantum technologies
phys.org/news/2026-11-scientists-magneti.excerpt: Researchers at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Ames National Laboratory have discovered a way to control the handedness of magnons, tiny magnetic waves that can carry information through materials. By changing the material's magnetic state with an external magnetic field, they were able to switch magnon behavior, a finding with potential applications in quantum information and quantum computing technologies. Their findings are published in Physical Review Letters.

phys.org/news/2026-11-classicalquantum-i.title: Classical–quantum light interactions could make complex quantum behavior easier to simulate
phys.org/news/2026-11-classicalquantum-i.excerpt: An international collaboration demonstrates that classical nonlinear dynamics can drive single- and two-photon states to thermalize, opening new avenues for simulating complex quantum many-body systems within accessible optical architectures.

phys.org/news/2026-11-ai-universal-highe.title: AI use is now universal in higher education. Why are universities failing to adapt?
phys.org/news/2026-11-ai-universal-highe.excerpt: Artificial intelligence use among university students is now near-universal in many countries. Yet, as of a year ago, fewer than one in five universities in a 90-country UNESCO survey had a formal AI policy.

phys.org/news/2026-11-earth-core-carbon-.title: Earth's 'core carbon' may have come from the far reaches of the solar system
phys.org/news/2026-11-earth-core-carbon-.excerpt: A new study suggests that most of Earth's carbon originated in the outer solar system and didn't arrive here until the late stages of planetary development. The study, led by researchers at Yale and Columbia, is based upon an analysis of magma droplets called "melt inclusions" from historic volcano eruptions in Hawaii, including the Keanakākoʻi eruptions from 1500 to 1840 and the Kīlauea Iki eruption in 1959.

phys.org/news/2026-11-poles-bacteria-ima.title: Poles of bacteria imaged in fine detail for the first time
phys.org/news/2026-11-poles-bacteria-ima.excerpt: The poles, or ends, of rod-shaped bacteria have been imaged at molecular resolution for the first time in a new study led by UCL (University College London) researchers. The study, published in the journal Nature Communications, used a new technique to keep live bacteria in place so the cells could be imaged without wriggling away.

phys.org/news/2026-11-approach-boosts-pl.title: New approach boosts plastic-eating enzyme's activity nearly tenfold
phys.org/news/2026-11-approach-boosts-pl.excerpt: Researchers from King's College London and Rutgers University in New Jersey created a modified enzyme (a protein that speeds up chemical reactions) that breaks down polyethylene terephthalate (PET) plastic 10 times quicker, using 10 times less enzyme. They accomplished this just by changing the liquid it works in and making small changes to the enzyme's structure.

phys.org/news/2026-11-financial-tout-sus.title: Financial institutions tout sustainability while still funding high-carbon projects, review finds
phys.org/news/2026-11-financial-tout-sus.excerpt: A review published in the International Journal of Managerial and Financial Accounting on the subject of greenwashing in financial services has found that financial institutions often claim environmental responsibility while continuing to finance high-carbon projects.

phys.org/news/2026-11-protein-rna-molecu.title: Protein-building RNA molecules reveal possible remnants of an ancestral genetic code
phys.org/news/2026-11-protein-rna-molecu.excerpt: The genetic code determines the correspondence between genetic instructions and amino acids—the building blocks that form proteins. How this correspondence arose is one of the major open questions in evolutionary biology. A study led by Dr. Lluís Ribas de Pouplana, ICREA researcher at IRB Barcelona, and Dr. Paul Schimmel, with the participation of researchers from MIT and Scripps Research, has identified conserved signals in transfer RNAs that could help reconstruct the early stages of this system.

phys.org/news/2026-11-webb-controversial.title: Webb's controversial 'little red dots' may finally have an explanation
phys.org/news/2026-11-webb-controversial.excerpt: Astronomers may have solved one of the biggest mysteries uncovered by NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), using sophisticated simulations to show that enigmatic objects known as "little red dots" (LRDs) are likely the birthplaces of the first supermassive black holes.

phys.org/news/2026-11-protein-tails-mosq.title: Protein tails help shape mosquito cell-to-cell channels
phys.org/news/2026-11-protein-tails-mosq.excerpt: Cells share small molecules with their neighbors through tiny tunnels made of proteins arranged in a ring. Research at Nagoya University suggests that the tails of the proteins must link up to form an inner ring for the tunnel to become evenly round—a previously unknown step in how these cell-to-cell connections are built.

phys.org/news/2026-11-howler-monkey-spec.title: Two new howler monkey species discovered in the Amazon after 85 years
phys.org/news/2026-11-howler-monkey-spec.excerpt: Genetic research has uncovered two previously unknown species of howler monkey living in the Amazon rainforest, confirming the world's largest tropical forest is more biodiverse than scientists thought.

phys.org/news/2026-11-archives-reveal-cl.title: Archives reveal how climate memories may reset with each generation
phys.org/news/2026-11-archives-reveal-cl.excerpt: The collective memory of floods and droughts influences where people settle, how they build and how they prepare for the next climatic extreme. Over decades, that memory can fade, and communities may return to places that once proved dangerous. How such memory decayed over centuries is hard to observe because the climate past societies experienced is usually known only from their own records.

phys.org/news/2026-11-method-tracking-cl.title: A new method for tracking climate change and air pollution
phys.org/news/2026-11-method-tracking-cl.excerpt: Two papers by Prof. Thomas A. Weber develop a rank-based method to track environmental change. They apply the idea to follow Geneva's warming climate, and generalize the approach to quantify shifts in spatial air-pollution exposure across Switzerland. The method compares observations with a historical baseline and shows how accounting for where people live changes the assessment of air-quality improvements.

phys.org/news/2026-11-gravitational-hint.title: Gravitational waves hint at black holes born from failed supernovae
phys.org/news/2026-11-gravitational-hint.excerpt: When the most massive stars in the universe die, they often detonate in fiery supernovae, dramatically blasting most of their matter into space. The remaining stellar cores collapse into neutron stars and, sometimes, black holes. However, theories suggest that some massive stars might die without a bang, instead directly collapsing inward to become neutron stars or black holes.

phys.org/news/2026-11-definition-sexual-.title: When the definition of sexual consent gets stretched
phys.org/news/2026-11-definition-sexual-.excerpt: Men in treatment for domestic violence have an elastic view of what constitutes consent in their partner, an UdeM study has found.

phys.org/news/2026-11-laser-reveal-forbi.title: Repeatable laser measurements reveal 'forbidden' vibrations in single molecules without destroying them
phys.org/news/2026-11-laser-reveal-forbi.excerpt: The possibility of controlling "forbidden" excitations of vibrations in molecules could form the basis of extremely accurate clocks, quantum bits and precise tests of the fundamental laws of physics. Researchers at the University of Basel have now identified and controlled such "forbidden" transitions in single isolated nitrogen molecules without destroying them.

phys.org/news/2026-11-airborne-imaging-e.title: Airborne imaging explores a mosaic of thawing permafrost
phys.org/news/2026-11-airborne-imaging-e.excerpt: Permafrost in many of Earth's northern regions is thawing, a process that unlocks greenhouse gases, threatens infrastructure, and could alter landscapes and ecosystems. The Arctic and subarctic are vast, and gaining a comprehensive picture of permafrost distribution is difficult, as it requires seeing under the ground. Now, with a new method that can map permafrost from the air, researchers may get a much more spatially cohesive view of permafrost thickness and distribution.

phys.org/news/2026-11-reef-biodiversity-.title: Reef biodiversity accounting to help scale up restoration
phys.org/news/2026-11-reef-biodiversity-.excerpt: To encourage new investments in more effective reef restoration activities, Australian scientists are recommending a new way of measuring biodiversity on coral reefs. A team of Australian environmental scientists led by James Cook University's distinguished professor Morgan Pratchett proposes the more rigorous and transparent framework in a paper published in the journal One Earth.

phys.org/news/2026-11-leader-language.ht.title: Leader still means man, and language does not change that, according to study
phys.org/news/2026-11-leader-language.ht.excerpt: Can gender-inclusive language weaken the deeply ingrained stereotype that a political leader is a man? A recent international study, conducted in 42 countries and involving researchers from SWPS University, shows that introducing such forms into language has little impact on how the public perceives political leaders.

phys.org/news/2026-11-deep-reefs-corals-.title: Deep reefs provide corals little refuge from extreme ocean heat
phys.org/news/2026-11-deep-reefs-corals-.excerpt: Once regarded as potential safe havens for corals in a warming climate, deep reefs, which lie at depths between 90 and 150 meters (295 and 490 feet), are no longer sheltered from increasingly intense marine heat waves, according to a new study in Geophysical Research Letters.

phys.org/news/2026-11-links-bacteria-was.title: Study finds links between bacteria in wastewater and chronic disease
phys.org/news/2026-11-links-bacteria-was.excerpt: Bacteria found in wastewater may provide clues about community health, including rates of chronic disease, health behaviors and social conditions, according to a recent study from The Ohio State University.

phys.org/news/2026-11-free-air-tv-failur.title: Free-to-air TV failures add to data costs for remote Australian First Nations households
phys.org/news/2026-11-free-air-tv-failur.excerpt: Almost two in three respondents surveyed in Australia's remote First Nations communities did not have working free-to-air television, a study has found.

phys.org/news/2026-11-qa-ai-major-world-.title: Q&A: 'AI has become a major force shaping our world,' says expert
phys.org/news/2026-11-qa-ai-major-world-.excerpt: Artificial intelligence is reshaping research, economies, and everyday life at a remarkable speed. In this interview accompanying the new AI100 report, Iyad Rahwan reflects on the rise of generative AI, the growing concentration of AI power, and the challenges facing societies worldwide. He also explains why Europe must seize this "Sputnik moment" and why he remains optimistic about AI's potential to accelerate scientific discovery.

phys.org/news/2026-11-archaeological-fis.title: Archaeological trap: Fish can make skeletons appear hundreds of years too old
phys.org/news/2026-11-archaeological-fis.excerpt: The Danish town of Svendborg was once home to a Franciscan monastery. As at other monasteries in Denmark, it was considered highly prestigious to be buried as close to the monastery church as possible, preferably inside the church itself, for instance near the chapter house or along the cloister.

phys.org/news/2026-11-phd-reciprocal-can.title: Ph.D. completion depends on reciprocal mix of candidate, supervision and institution, review finds
phys.org/news/2026-11-phd-reciprocal-can.excerpt: Low Ph.D. completion rates remain a challenge in higher education, reflecting a complex interplay of individual, supervisory and institutional factors. Despite extensive research, few reviews have investigated the factors related to Ph.D. completion, with most focusing on isolated aspects, such as supervision or mental health.

phys.org/news/2026-11-purple-bacteria-in.title: Purple bacteria turn CO₂ and other industrial waste products into valuable supplement ingredients
phys.org/news/2026-11-purple-bacteria-in.excerpt: Scientists are always on the lookout for more efficient ways to make useful products and ingredients. Now, researchers from the University of Valladolid in Spain have successfully used a type of purple bacteria to make CoQ10 and carotenoid pigments from CO₂ and other ingredients found in industrial waste streams. The new study is published in the journal Environmental Science & Technology.

phys.org/news/2026-11-landfill-leachate-.title: Landfill leachate tests reveal divergent fates of biodegradable plastics
phys.org/news/2026-11-landfill-leachate-.excerpt: Even among plastics labeled "biodegradable," some break down readily while others persist for long periods. In experiments using landfill leachate, a collaborative research team led by the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) demonstrated these differences and identified candidate microorganisms and enzymes potentially involved in plastic degradation.

livescience.com/physics-mathematics/hidd.title: Gravity can reconnect like the sun's magnetic field, a fresh look at Einstein's equations reveals
livescience.com/physics-mathematics/hidd.excerpt: A fresh look at Einstein's equations suggests that gravity can sometimes snap and reconnect, similar to magnetic field lines on the sun. The findings hint at a new way that gravity and matter can trade energy.

noirlab.edu/public/news/noirlab2627.title: Science Release: Astronomers Discover Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, the Oldest Compact Quasar Pair in the Universe
noirlab.edu/public/news/noirlab2627.excerpt: The oldest pair of compact quasars ever observed has been found only 900 million years after the Big Bang. Scientists say there is no theoretical explanation for how the pair of actively feeding black holes grew so massive at such an early time in the history of the Universe. The pair of quasars has been given the Hawaiian nickname Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua.

jpl.nasa.gov/news/nasa-invites-media-pub.title: NASA Invites Media, Public to Join Voyager 1 One-Light Day Activities
jpl.nasa.gov/news/nasa-invites-media-pub.excerpt: Launched nearly 50 years ago in 1977, NASA’s Voyager 1 on Wednesday, Nov. 18 will have traveled one light-day from Earth, which is more than 16 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers).

space.com/entertainment/anthony-mackie-a.excerpt: We hooked up with Mackie, DeBose, and Lequizamo to learn more about this renaissance of audio dramas and what attracted them to board Weir's sci-fi thriller.

space.com/space-exploration/on-this-day-.excerpt: On Nov. 10, 2013, Europe's GOCE satellite fell to Earth after four years in orbit mapping the planet's gravitational field. Here's why it mattered.

space.com/astronomy/exoplanets/a-distant.excerpt: Astronomers have solved the mystery of an exoplanet that "disappeared" after seven years of observations.

space.com/entertainment/space-movies-sho.excerpt: How to stream "We Chose to Go to the Moon", a live broadcast of the dazzling new stage retelling of the space race story.

space.com/news/live/spacex-starship-flig.excerpt: Follow live updates as SpaceX attempts its Starship Flight 15 test flight with first double landings.

space.com/astronomy/uranus/scientists-ma.title: Uranus has a weird magnetic field that's stumped scientists for 40 years — we may finally know why
space.com/astronomy/uranus/scientists-ma.excerpt: The lopsided magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune could be the product of extreme conditions inside the planets, increasing the electrical conductivity that enhances the dynamo effect.

space.com/space-exploration/launches-spa.title: Were there 'lost cosmonauts' in the early Soviet space program?
space.com/space-exploration/launches-spa.excerpt: At the height of the Cold War, two amateur radio operators alleged they intercepted signals from Soviet cosmonauts who perished during missions that remained secret.

universetoday.com/articles/automated-ass.title: Automated Assembly in Space is the Future and NOM4D is Showing the Way
universetoday.com/articles/automated-ass.excerpt: The ability to build large structures in space is maturing. The ISS, Mir, and Tiangong were built in space from pre-constructed modules, but a new program called NOM4D is taking space construction to the next level. It recently showed that a simple robot can create truss-like structures in space from premade components. Is the sky the limit for NOM4D?

universetoday.com/articles/alma-reveals-.title: ALMA Reveals a Jet of Cool Gas from a Microquasar
universetoday.com/articles/alma-reveals-.excerpt: There's a strange gamma-ray emitter in the Large Magellanic Cloud that has astronomers stumped about its source. It lies within the ashes left behind by a supernova that created a compact object that's part of the system. The supernova remnant provides some evidence for the emissions, but not the whole story.

universetoday.com/articles/breakthrough-.title: First Direct Measurement of Cosmic Hydrogen Could Change How We Map the Universe
universetoday.com/articles/breakthrough-.excerpt: The MeerKLASS international collaboration achieves the first direct measurement of the large-scale clustering of cosmic hydrogen in the Universe.

universetoday.com/articles/why-aging-sta.title: Why Aging Stars Suffer A Sudden Luminosity Dip
universetoday.com/articles/why-aging-sta.excerpt: When low-mass stars like our Sun age, they leave the main sequence and follow the Red Giant Branch. As they ascend this branch, their luminosity steadily increases. But there's a sort of hiccup in the path called the RGB luminosity bump, where their luminosity suddenly dips. Astrophysicists have struggle to explain this, but one astrophysicist might have the answer.

earthsky.org/space/voyager-1-1-light-day.title: Celebrate as Voyager 1 reaches 1 light-day from Earth! Here’s how
earthsky.org/space/voyager-1-1-light-day.excerpt: The Voyager 1 spacecraft -- launched from Earth in 1977 -- will become the 1st human-made object to reach 1 light-day from Earth on November 18. The post Celebrate as Voyager 1 reaches 1 light-day from Earth! Here’s how first appeared on EarthSky .

phys.org/news/2026-11-covid-added-tax-si.title: New study shows COVID value-added tax cut significantly boosted private consumption
phys.org/news/2026-11-covid-added-tax-si.excerpt: In summer 2020, the German federal government lowered value-added tax from 19% to 16% for half a year as part of its COVID economic stimulus package. A new study, recently published in the journal Review of Economic Studies, uses survey data, data on retail purchases and an economic model to show the extent to which this measure influenced private consumption. The study found that lower-wealth households, as well as younger and middle-aged households, particularly benefited, regardless of their level of financial literacy.

phys.org/news/2026-11-coyotes-permanent-.title: Coyotes are likely a permanent fixture on the Outer Banks of North Carolina
phys.org/news/2026-11-coyotes-permanent-.excerpt: A new study reveals that coyote populations on the Outer Banks persist despite ongoing removal programs, posing a continued threat to shore-nesting birds and protected sea turtles. The study is the first in-depth assessment of coyote populations on barrier islands and has ramifications for understanding how coyotes may impact these and other barrier island ecosystems.

phys.org/news/2026-11-framework-products.title: Simplified framework could make products' environmental impacts easier to assess
phys.org/news/2026-11-framework-products.excerpt: Life cycle assessment is used to quantify the environmental impact of products and services and forms an important basis for political decisions. However, the necessary data is always difficult to capture completely. A study by the Paul Scherrer Institute PSI now shows that four established hybrid methods can be reduced to just two: a first step towards open-source software that could enable such analyses even without in-depth mathematical knowledge.

phys.org/news/2026-11-mental-health-app-.title: Mental health app may help unemployed people find jobs, six-week trial suggests
phys.org/news/2026-11-mental-health-app-.excerpt: Losing a job can be a life-shattering experience. And when depression complicates a job search, unemployment can become a vicious cycle. Now, a Northwestern University–led clinical trial suggests a new intervention may break that cycle: a phone app, named DRIVEN, that combines weekly self-guided mental health exercises (to reduce stress and increase motivation) with job-seeking strategies.

phys.org/news/2026-11-tool-biodiversity-.title: A new tool makes biodiversity conservation planning more efficient and reproducible
phys.org/news/2026-11-tool-biodiversity-.excerpt: ZonationR is a new tool that simplifies the use of Zonation to identify priority areas for biodiversity conservation. It brings all stages of the conservation planning analysis together in one automated and reproducible workflow and helps users systematically explore and compare alternative conservation scenarios.

phys.org/news/2026-11-genetic-ancestry-p.title: Genetic ancestry plays a key role in the migration of Cory's shearwaters
phys.org/news/2026-11-genetic-ancestry-p.excerpt: To what extent do genes influence the migratory routes of birds? The factors that determine the long-distance migrations of seabirds are not yet fully understood. Now, a study published in the journal Molecular Ecology reveals that, in the case of Cory's shearwater, an individual's genetic ancestry is a more significant factor in their migratory decisions than their social environment in the breeding colony.

phys.org/news/2026-11-earliest-compact-q.title: Earliest known compact quasar pair poses a black hole growth puzzle
phys.org/news/2026-11-earliest-compact-q.excerpt: The oldest pair of compact quasars ever observed has been found only 900 million years after the Big Bang. Scientists say there is no theoretical explanation for how the pair of actively feeding black holes grew so massive at such an early time in the history of the universe. The pair of quasars has been given the Hawaiian nickname Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua.

phys.org/news/2026-11-iron-sulfur-framew.title: New organic iron-sulfur framework boosts photosynthesis and carbon fixation
phys.org/news/2026-11-iron-sulfur-framew.excerpt: Iron-sulfur clusters are ancient protein cofactors that are essential for electron transport, enzyme catalysis and photosynthesis. However, their sensitivity to oxygen and inherent instability have long hindered their practical application.

phys.org/news/2026-11-ripples-space-reve.title: How ripples in space-time can reveal new exoplanets
phys.org/news/2026-11-ripples-space-reve.excerpt: The LISA (Laser Interferometer Space Antenna) observatory, now in development, will detect gravitational waves, the tiny ripples in space-time caused by orbiting masses. Now two studies led by NASA astrophysicists show in new detail how LISA could reveal a new and unique population of exoplanets—worlds beyond our solar system—throughout our galaxy.

phys.org/news/2026-11-european-eels-tran.title: European eels transmit a herpesvirus through bites, revealing another route for fish infections
phys.org/news/2026-11-european-eels-tran.excerpt: Contrary to what was previously believed, viruses infecting fish are not transmitted exclusively through water acting as an abiotic vector. A team of researchers from the University of Liège has demonstrated that a virus affecting European eels can spread very efficiently through biting during aggressive interactions between individuals.

phys.org/news/2026-11-ai-aid-chemistry-r.title: Where AI can aid chemistry research and where reliability falls short
phys.org/news/2026-11-ai-aid-chemistry-r.excerpt: Researchers from the Skoltech AI Center, together with colleagues from the Zelinsky Institute of Organic Chemistry of the Russian Academy of Sciences, ITMO University and other institutions, have published a paper in Chemical Society Reviews that examines where AI produces measurable value in a chemical research workflow, how to assess its reliability and why a strong benchmark result does not necessarily translate into laboratory performance.

phys.org/news/2026-11-repurposing-intern.title: Repurposing the internet's backbone to advance whale monitoring
phys.org/news/2026-11-repurposing-intern.excerpt: Bioacoustics researcher Léa Bouffaut, at the Cornell K. Lisa Yang Center for Conservation Bioacoustics, has spent the past several years eavesdropping on the conversations of whales. But instead of using underwater microphones like other marine scientists, she listens by tapping into fiber-optic cables lying on the ocean floor—a powerful tool to aid in marine mammal conservation.

phys.org/news/2026-11-anemone-spurs-stro.title: Anemone bleaching spurs stronger home defense and more aggression among clownfish
phys.org/news/2026-11-anemone-spurs-stro.excerpt: Marine heat waves and anemone bleaching are altering clownfish behavior, making clownfish more defensive of their host and more aggressive toward one another, new research reveals.

phys.org/news/2026-11-rerouting-ships-wh.title: Rerouting ships to avoid killing whale sharks has little cost, study finds
phys.org/news/2026-11-rerouting-ships-wh.excerpt: Redirecting shipping traffic to avoid collisions with whale sharks has very little impact on fuel use, according to new research led by the University of Southampton published in Royal Society Open Science.

phys.org/news/2026-11-ancient-reveal-ear.title: Ancient rocks reveal when Earth's tectonic engine 'switched on'
phys.org/news/2026-11-ancient-reveal-ear.excerpt: Scientists have identified a major turning point in Earth's geological history, when the processes shaping the planet's crust changed dramatically and began to resemble the plate tectonics we see today—about 2.5 billion years ago.

phys.org/news/2026-11-high-disadvantaged.title: High-achieving disadvantaged students are far less likely to take and pass entrance exams for selective schools
phys.org/news/2026-11-high-disadvantaged.excerpt: Disadvantaged students are less likely than their more advantaged peers with similar attainment to take and pass entrance exams for selective schools, and introducing an opt-out system for the tests would only deliver a small boost.

phys.org/news/2026-11-scientists-anchor-.title: Scientists anchor first scientific animal name to a modern-day spider
phys.org/news/2026-11-scientists-anchor-.excerpt: Scientists led by the Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History have restored the physical reference of one of the most historically significant names in biology. In a paper published in Taxonomy, researchers designated a new type specimen, or neotype, for Araneus angulatus, the first animal species described using binomial nomenclature, the two-part naming system that scientists use today to identify and classify living organisms. The designation reconnects the name to a physical specimen decades after the original name-bearing spiders disappeared.

phys.org/news/2026-11-rein-emissions-pow.title: Governments are failing to rein in emissions from their own power plants, analysis finds
phys.org/news/2026-11-rein-emissions-pow.excerpt: World leaders meeting at the annual U.N. climate summit in November 2026 are wrestling with a persistent challenge: how to get countries to follow through on their commitments to reduce greenhouse gas emissions that are warming the planet.

phys.org/news/2026-11-gamma-brittle-biop.title: Gamma radiation transforms brittle bioplastic into 'superstructure' hydrogel
phys.org/news/2026-11-gamma-brittle-biop.excerpt: Biomaterials engineers have created a "superstructure" hydrogel that could be an eco-friendly tool used in medical technologies and as a recovery aid for surgical procedures. The research is published in the journal Macromolecular Rapid Communications.

phys.org/news/2026-11-pet-skin-pose-thre.title: The pet and skin trades pose little threat to reptile species, analyses suggest
phys.org/news/2026-11-pet-skin-pose-thre.excerpt: Reptiles are captivating creatures—so captivating that people keep them as pets, or wear clothes and carry handbags fashioned from their patterned skins.

phys.org/news/2026-11-psychology-electri.title: The psychology of saving electricity: How comparisons can curb consumption
phys.org/news/2026-11-psychology-electri.excerpt: Simple psychological interventions are often enough to encourage people to change their behavior—and this is also true when it comes to saving electricity. A new study by Mannheim-based consumer psychologist Dr. Yavor Paunov and colleagues shows that comparing one's own electricity consumption with that of others as well as practical energy-saving tips can help reduce energy consumption.

phys.org/news/2026-11-microscopy-sharpen.title: Microscopy upgrade sharpens images fivefold without sacrificing tissue imaging depth
phys.org/news/2026-11-microscopy-sharpen.excerpt: Researchers at Texas A&M University have cracked a problem that has limited biological imaging for years: seeing fine cellular detail while looking deep inside living tissue. The new microscopy technique resolves structures smaller than 100 nanometers, roughly a thousand times thinner than a human hair, without giving up the ability to image deep into intact samples.

phys.org/news/2026-11-molecules-secret-m.title: Water molecules turn out to be secret messengers for magnetism
phys.org/news/2026-11-molecules-secret-m.excerpt: Water is not usually thought of as a magnetic material. But a new study led by researchers at Tohoku University's Institute of Multidisciplinary Research for Advanced Materials, in collaboration with National Taipei University of Technology (Taipei Tech), has found that tiny shifts in the orientation of water molecules can flip on magnetic partnerships between metal ions that are not even directly bonded to each other.

phys.org/news/2026-11-harnessing-laser-n.title: Harnessing laser nuisance achieves record resolution for atomic measurements
phys.org/news/2026-11-harnessing-laser-n.excerpt: A shoebox-sized color detection device could enable precise measurements at record resolution, according to new research led by Adelaide University. An international team exploited an integrating sphere—a highly reflective hollow cavity that causes light to bounce around inside many times before exiting—to demonstrate a device that can measure the color (wavelength) composition of light with extreme precision at a resolution of just 6 femtometers.

phys.org/news/2026-11-prison-analysis-lo.title: Prison data analysis finds choosing lowest reoffending risk scores preserves overall accuracy
phys.org/news/2026-11-prison-analysis-lo.excerpt: Whether an individual reoffends after their release from prison or is successfully rehabilitated depends on several factors. When assessing the risk of recidivism, all of these are taken into account—both by human experts and by machine learning models. If several equally reliable computational models produce different risk ratings, the lowest value should be used for the individual concerned, suggest Ashwin Singh (TU Wien) and Carlos Castillo (ICREA/Universitat Pompeu Fabra).

phys.org/news/2026-11-sexual-violence-pl.title: Sexual violence can hide in plain sight at music festivals, according to new study
phys.org/news/2026-11-sexual-violence-pl.excerpt: The pressure to maintain an atmosphere of fun and escapism can make it harder for festival organizations to acknowledge and respond to harm, while frontline workers are left dealing with its consequences, a new study finds.

phys.org/news/2026-11-seafloor-clay-reve.title: Seafloor clay reveals past dramatic ice loss in West Antarctica
phys.org/news/2026-11-seafloor-clay-reve.excerpt: Scientists have discovered the best evidence yet to show that West Antarctica's most vulnerable ice streams—including its giant Thwaites Glacier—repeatedly collapsed and retreated far inland during natural warm periods of the last 800,000 years.

phys.org/news/2026-11-swordfish-deep-oce.title: Swordfish may be using deep dives to navigate the open ocean
phys.org/news/2026-11-swordfish-deep-oce.excerpt: Swordfish spend much of their time hunting prey about 600 meters (1,970 feet) below the surface in the ocean twilight zone, but occasionally, they reach depths of more than 1,000 meters (3,280 feet). Now, scientists from the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) are investigating what may be behind these extreme dives.

phys.org/news/2026-11-ai-generated-molec.title: AI-generated molecular fingerprints help identify existing compounds with therapeutic potential
phys.org/news/2026-11-ai-generated-molec.excerpt: Health care researchers have long sought to harness the power of computing to design molecules that bind to specific receptors and can be used as targeted treatments for diseases. Even with the increasing sophistication of artificial intelligence, however, this technological promise has yet to be realized.

phys.org/news/2026-11-3d-view-babesiosis.title: Detailed 3D view of babesiosis parasite's ribosome could guide development of targeted treatments
phys.org/news/2026-11-3d-view-babesiosis.excerpt: A new study has revealed a three-dimensional, near-atomic-resolution view of the ribosome from Babesia divergens, one of several Babesia species known to infect humans and cause babesiosis. The structural insights from this close-up view could help researchers identify parasite-specific features that may be exploited for future drug development.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261110.title: Scientists discover a giant 66-pound rodent that lived 34 million years ago
sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261110.excerpt: Scientists have uncovered fossils of a giant rodent that lived in Thailand 34 million years ago, revealing that enormous rodents evolved much earlier than previously thought. Named Yakamys sirindhornae, the ancient animal may have weighed around 66 pounds, roughly twice as much as other known rodents of its time.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261109.title: 237-million-year-old fossils reveal a bizarre armored sea amphibian
sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261109.excerpt: A bizarre, heavily armored amphibian roamed the oceans 237 million years ago, despite the fact that modern amphibians cannot survive entirely in saltwater. Discovered in China, the giant salamander-sized creature may be the first known amphibian to have adapted to a fully marine existence.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261108.title: Astronomers discover hidden alien planet in James Webb images
sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261108.excerpt: A breakthrough in telescope imaging could reveal countless alien worlds that have been hiding in plain sight. Scientists developed a new technique that uses a digital twin of the James Webb Space Telescope to remove the overwhelming glare of stars, making faint exoplanets two to 15 times easier to detect than with conventional methods. The technology has already uncovered a previously hidden planet in existing telescope data and could reveal many more.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261106.title: Scientists discover why some mosquitoes love you and others don't
sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261106.excerpt: A surprising new study reveals that mosquitoes have very different tastes in humans, with each species attracted to its own combination of skin odors, chemicals, and bacteria. The discovery challenges the idea of a universal mosquito magnet and could lead to more effective repellents against dangerous disease-spreading mosquitoes.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261105.title: A mysterious 93-billion-mile cosmic structure may be the wreckage of colliding worlds
sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261105.excerpt: NASA's Hubble Space Telescope has revealed surprising new details about a mysterious, 93-billion-mile-long cloud of dark, fluffy dust that may have formed when massive planetary bodies collided. The discovery challenges previous assumptions about the structure and offers new clues about the violent birth of planetary systems.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261105.title: Comets may have destroyed life's ingredients instead of delivering them to Earth
sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261105.excerpt: A century-old theory about the origins of life on Earth may be wrong. New research from the University of Cambridge suggests that comets traveled too fast and struck at unfavorable angles for the fragile molecules needed for life to survive, making successful delivery extraordinarily unlikely. Surprisingly, Mars may have had a better chance of receiving these cosmic ingredients, although even there the odds were slim. The findings point toward asteroids or chemical processes on Earth as more plausible sources of life's building blocks.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261105.title: Paleontologists discover “one-in-a-million” fossil with 450-million-year-old soft tissue
sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261105.excerpt: Scientists have discovered a remarkably preserved 450-million-year-old fossil containing soft tissues from an ancient starfish relative, revealing unexpected details about marine life more than 200 million years before dinosaurs existed. Found in a museum collection, the extraordinarily rare specimen offers new clues about how Earth's earliest reef animals fed, survived, and evolved.

arxiv.org/abs/2611.12923.title: Spacetime contactability in Galactic civilization networks: Contact counts and percolation
arxiv.org/abs/2611.12923.excerpt:
arXiv:2611.12923v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The number of Galactic civilizations does not determine whether they are in contact. Allowing civilizations to appear at different times separates listening, audibility, mutual-listening, and relay networks, with a distinct reply-closing condition requiring a return signal within the sender's lifetime. For each network we derive the contact counts and estimate the connectivity threshold in a uniform population, then apply the results to a structured Galactic disc, separating the detection range $d_{\rm max}$ from the light horizon $cL$ through $\chi=d_{\rm max}/cL$. The contactability is $\eta=\pi n d_{\rm max}^{2}$, where $n$ is the active civilization surface density. Averaged over civilization appearances, the lifetime listening count is $2\eta$ for all $\chi$ and, at fixed detection range, for any lifetime distribution. Audibility and mutual-listening counts sum to $4\eta$, but connectivity depends on threshold behavior rather than counts alone. As $\chi\rightarrow0$, the listening threshold decreases from the coeval value $4.51$ to $1.32\pm0.01$. Assuming an ideal complete survey, our own non-detection gives the reference bound $\eta(R_0)\le2.75$ at the Sun's Galactocentric radius. This benchmark lies above the listening, audibility and relay thresholds throughout the range studied. Unlike the coeval model, the spacetime model can satisfy both this benchmark and a local connectivity criterion, moving the local-contact frontier outward by $3.2$ kpc. Under the same benchmark, civilizations hear at most $5.5$ others on average, while the mean reply-closing count falls below unity for $\chi\gtrsim1$. Contact may therefore be common even when completed replies remain rare.

arxiv.org/abs/2611.12945.title: Early X-ray emission as an observational diagnostic of gamma-ray burst progenitors
arxiv.org/abs/2611.12945.excerpt:
arXiv:2611.12945v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Identifying the progenitors of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) from the properties of their early high-energy emission detected by wide-field satellites is crucial for advancing our understanding of GRB physics and for multi-messenger astronomy. Current classification methods, which rely primarily on prompt emission properties, exhibit large scatter and are challenged by recently detected events. In this Letter, we propose a new method to classify GRB progenitors using their early X-ray emission, which is detectable by current wide-field X-ray monitors. We performed a systematic time-resolved spectral analysis of the X-ray steep decay phase for a sample of 23 collapsar-driven GRB candidates detected by the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory. We fitted the spectra over the $0.3 - 150 \, \rm keV$ energy range using both a physical synchrotron model and the empirical Band function, allowing us to constrain the spectral peak energy and the bolometric flux. We find a correlation between the rest-frame synchrotron cooling frequency, $\nu_{c,z}$, and the isotropic-equivalent luminosity, $L_{\rm iso}$, that is clearly separated from the $\nu_{c,z} - L_{\rm iso}$ relation followed by merger-driven GRB candidates. A similarly distinct separation is found in the correlation between the rest-frame peak energy, $E_{p,z}$, and $L_{\rm iso}$ obtained with the Band model. Finally, we provide a prescription for classifying fast X-ray transients detected by the Wide-field X-ray Telescope aboard the Einstein Probe mission, as its narrow energy range ($0.5 - 4 \, \rm keV$) limits spectral modelling to a simple power law. We show that the photon index and X-ray luminosity of the steep decay spectra clearly separate collapsar- and merger-driven candidate events, making them powerful diagnostics of GRB progenitors.

arxiv.org/abs/2611.12973.title: Standalone Validation of a Pulsar Evolution Subroutine for NBODY6++GPU: Seven Test Scenarios
arxiv.org/abs/2611.12973.excerpt:
arXiv:2611.12973v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Pulsars in globular clusters provide critical constraints on the evolution of compact objects. However, the treatment of neutron stars in standard N-body codes is outdated, and requires a better implementation of magnetic field decay, spin evolution, and accretion driven recycling that shape their observable properties. We present a standalone validation of a pulsar evolution subroutine for NBODY6++GPU, systematically tested across seven controlled scenarios prior to integration into full cluster simulations. These scenarios isolate distinct evolutionary regimes, including young pulsar spin down, millisecond pulsar weak torque evolution, accretion driven recycling in X-ray binaries, environmental torques in dense cores, wide binary systems, and compact binaries in the dipole spin-down regime. Through two separate numerical implementations, we achieve cross validation demonstrating better than 0.1% agreement across all physical quantities and timescales. Our validation confirms that analytical solutions are reproduced with high precision for isolated pulsars, gigayear scale evolution (tau_c ~ 1.0 Gyr) matches observations of millisecond pulsars in clusters like 47 Tucanae, and accretion driven recycling operates with physically realistic timescales, yielding a final period of 1.0 ms and a period derivative of approximately -5.9e-19 s/s, with accretion dominance by a factor of about 14. We demonstrate that environmental torques remain negligible even in the densest cluster environments, while compact binary spin down is validated; gravitational wave orbital decay is deferred to future work. All validation codes, test suites, and integration instructions are publicly available to support future applications.

arxiv.org/abs/2611.13033.title: Mitigating oscillatory systematics in MeerKLASS L-band H i intensity maps
arxiv.org/abs/2611.13033.excerpt:
arXiv:2611.13033v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: HI intensity mapping is a promising probe of the large-scale structure of the Universe, but is limited by foregrounds and instrumental systematics. For the MeerKAT Large Area Synoptic Survey (MeerKLASS) L-band data, it is found that emission line stacking measurement reveals a type of systematics related to the instrument beam. Using simulations with a full-sky electromagnetic beam model, we show that the chromaticity and sidelobes of the MeerKAT beam modulate the frequency-smooth foreground emission and introduce oscillating structures that persist after foreground removal. The beam rotates with respect to the sky between two types of scans, and combining datasets with different beam orientations before foreground cleaning makes the residuals stronger. In MeerKLASS L-band data, processing these two types of scans separately significantly suppresses the oscillating residuals while preserving the stacked HI signal. The ratio of the HI signal amplitude to the systematic fluctuation amplitude increases by 81%. We find an oscillating structure in PCA mode 11 in our previous data processing, but simply removing this mode does not improve the stacked spectrum due to the signal loss. Our strategy can help mitigate spectral ripples that are induced by the beam in future MeerKAT and SKA-Mid surveys.

arxiv.org/abs/2611.13035.title: The Ordinary Days of Extraordinary Blazar 3C 454.3
arxiv.org/abs/2611.13035.excerpt:
arXiv:2611.13035v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The blazar 3C 454.3 (z = 0.859) is one of the brightest and most variable flat-spectrum radio quasars in the sky. Here, we present a multi-wavelength analysis of this enigmatic object in its quiescent states during June 2022 and May 2023 coincident with its first X-ray polarimetric and hard X-ray observations with International X-ray Polarimetric Explorer (IXPE) and Nuclear Spectroscopic Telescope Array (NuSTAR). Though no X-ray polarization was detected, NuSTAR detected the source on all occasions during this period. We generated five broadband spectral energy distributions (SEDs)of the blazar using quasi-simultaneous observations taken with the Fermi-Large Area Telescope, NuSTAR, and Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory. The hard X-ray flux measured by NuSTAR exhibited mild flux variations. The SEDs were modeled with a one-zone leptonic emission framework using the JetSet package. The optical-ultraviolet spectrum of 3C 454.3 revealed an upturn which we reproduced with the standard accretion disk model. The X-ray to gamma-ray spectrum of 3C 454 was found to be well explained by the external Compton (EC) process with the seed photons provided by the BLR and accretion disk. These results provide intriguing clues about the multi-wavelength behavior of 3C 454.3 during its quiescent activity state.

arxiv.org/abs/2611.13060.title: Aster: A Flexible and Robust Collection of Numerical Tools for N-Body Problems
arxiv.org/abs/2611.13060.excerpt:
arXiv:2611.13060v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The Aster library is an open-source collection of numerical tools designed for large-scale gravitational N-body simulations. Aster provides a flexible environment to its users, enabling it to be used in the analysis of a broad range of astrophysical problems. The library implements efficient force calculation algorithms, including a spatial tree solver optimized with coordinate-dependent identifiers, which has been fine-tuned for both CPU and GPU architectures. Despite its high degree of modularity, many parts of the library have been optimized with SIMD instructions, heavy parallelization, and support on dedicated hardware. Aster also offers a wide variety of numerical symplectic integrators, such as SABA (from first to tenth order), the classic leapfrog algorithm, and the more advanced Wisdom-Holman (WH) integrator, while also providing a vast collection of mathematical tools, e.g., post-newtonian expansions (1PN, 2PN, 2.5PN), data collection and graphing systems, a built-in renderer, and presets for faster instantiation of large amounts of bodies. In this work we will discuss in depth the details of each module as well as the results of several performance- and accuracy-related tests, probing the library's capabilities in different physical applications.

arxiv.org/abs/2611.13064.title: Mars Seed: A Reference Architecture for Biomanufacturing Habitats from Martian Resources
arxiv.org/abs/2611.13064.excerpt:
arXiv:2611.13064v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Human exploration of Mars will require enormous quantities of materials for the first crewed missions and substantially more for permanent habitation, making flexible and scalable technologies for in situ resource utilization (ISRU), including biological ISRU, of significant interest. However, no existing mission architecture quantitatively evaluates whether in situ biomanufacturing can realistically deliver materials at the scales required for human settlement. Here, we present Mars Seed, an end-to-end reference architecture for using biomanufacturing to produce bioplastics at scale entirely from in situ resources on Mars. We provide a complete analysis of a space bioprocess in which feedstocks are generated entirely from Martian resources, converted biologically into polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB) bioplastic, and purified to produce material suitable for constructing human habitats. We show that the upfront power and upmass costs of deploying the equipment required for this bioprocess are recovered within two synodic periods relative to Earth-shipped alternatives. Further, because the process relies entirely on feedstocks sourced from Martian materials, production can continue until equipment failure without requiring additional materials from Earth, enabling scalable conversion of local resources into useful materials. Mars Seed demonstrates that biological ISRU can be mass- and power-competitive with Earth-shipped alternatives, establishing biomanufacturing as a practical component of Mars mission architecture rather than an aspirational capability.

arxiv.org/abs/2611.13072.title: STarlight Acquisition and Reflection toward Interferometry (STARI) mission
arxiv.org/abs/2611.13072.excerpt:
arXiv:2611.13072v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We introduce the NASA-funded mission STARI (STarlight Acquisition and Reflection toward Interferometry), a two-spacecraft technology demonstrator for future long-baseline interferometers. STARI will perform, to our knowledge, the first in-space transfer of starlight between free-flying spacecraft, a critical step toward long-baseline space interferometry. Two propulsive 8U CubeSats in low Earth orbit will fly in formation with separations up to 200 m: one relays a narrow stellar beam to the other, where an off-axis parabola reimages it into a single-mode fiber. Using differential GNSS, visible LED beacons, and fast-steering mirrors in closed-loop control, we aim to sustain diffraction-limited, high-throughput fiber coupling during formation flight. STARI, targeting launch in 2029, is designed to mature key technologies needed for future mission concepts such as the Large Interferometer for Exoplanets (LIFE), which would seek atmospheric biomarkers on nearby Earth-like exoplanets.

arxiv.org/abs/2611.13082.title: The Impact of a Magnetic Field on stochastically generated g-modes
arxiv.org/abs/2611.13082.excerpt:
arXiv:2611.13082v1 Announce Type: new
