The final ray-traced spectrum, computed through photoionization code with Comptonization, accounts for both: emitted and reflected components. As a result, the strength of the SXE depends on the radial extend of the warm corona, i.e., its outer edge. We show that the radial transition from warm corona to disk atmosphere is governed by line cooling. By moving away from a central black hole Compton cooling is gradually replaced by line cooling, and the temperature drops sharply in vertical direction at a narrow iron ionization front, where iron ions Fe \textsc{xxv}--Fe \textsc{xxvi} recombine to Fe \textsc{xvii}. Notably, this transition takes place at a particular value of internal heating $\approx 1.6 \times 10^{-23}$ erg cm$^{3}$ s$^{-1}$, regardless of the Eddington ratio. We show, that at the given metal abundance, the SXE emitting area is larger for a higher accretion rate, in agreement with recent findings in changing look AGN. The overall emission spectrum from a warm corona is featureless, and the only iron K$_{\alpha}$ line comes from a reflection. The line is stronger and more gravitationally distorted for a lower accretion rate, which is a direct result of the size of the warm corona. Furthermore, by increasing the iron abundance, the iron ionization front moves closer towards black hole, and a stronger iron line complex is emitted locally.

arxiv.org/abs/2611.12881.title: The Brown Dwarf Desert is a Mass-Ratio Desert: Astrometric Demographics of 63,254 Stars
arxiv.org/abs/2611.12881.excerpt:
arXiv:2611.12881v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Brown dwarfs are rare as close companions to stars compared to planets and stellar companions, a paucity known as the brown dwarf desert. Whether the desert sits at a fixed companion mass or a fixed companion-to-star mass-ratio $q$ has been difficult to test, because microlensing, radial velocities, and direct imaging have sampled comparatively narrow slices of stellar mass and separation. Here we apply a novel joint-modelling method to Hipparcos and Gaia DR2/DR3 astrometry from 63,254 stars to complete this picture with a sample 1-2 orders of magnitude larger than those of previous wide-orbit demographic studies. For the first time, we present a single survey that measures occurrence rates of both planetary and stellar companions on 3--94 yr orbits ($\sim$2--20\,au) across host masses from M dwarfs to B stars. We find that the desert is a mass-ratio feature: companions are strongly depleted at $q\approx2\%$ independent of stellar mass from M to B stars, and a desert at fixed companion mass is excluded. Furthermore, we find a positive trend in occurrence with metallicity below the mass-ratio desert, but a negative trend above. The desert therefore separates two distinct populations, plausibly two formation channels, that each scale with stellar mass: the lightest stellar-like companions of K stars ($\sim13 \, M_{jup}$) are less massive than the heaviest planet-like companions of B stars ($\sim27, M_{jup}$), which continue well beyond the deuterium-burning limit. Mass-ratio, not mass, is therefore the physically meaningful boundary between planets and their stellar-like counterparts.

arxiv.org/abs/2510.16341.title: Investigating production of TeV-scale muons in extensive air shower at 2400 m underground
arxiv.org/abs/2510.16341.excerpt:
arXiv:2510.16341v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Deep underground experiments present a new avenue to probe the first interactions in extensive air showers or hadronic interactions in the extreme forward phase space. The China Jinping Underground Laboratory, characterized by a vertical rock overburden of 2,400 m, provides an exceptionally effective shield against cosmic muons with energies below 3 TeV. The surviving high-energy muons, produced in the first interactions of extensive air showers, open a unique observational window into primary cosmic rays from tens of TeV up to the PeV scale and beyond. This distinctive feature also enables detailed studies of charged hadron production in the earliest stages of shower development. Using 1,338.6 live days of data collected with a one-ton prototype detector for the Jinping Neutrino Experiment, we measured the underground muon flux originating from air showers. The results show discrepancies of about 40% corresponding to significances of more than 2$\sigma$, relative to predictions from several leading hadronic interaction models. We interpret these findings from two complementary perspectives: (i) by adopting the expected cosmic-ray spectra, we constrain the modeling of the first hadronic interactions in air showers and provide novel insights into resolving the long-standing muon puzzle; and (ii) by assuming specific hadronic interaction models, we infer the mass composition of cosmic rays, and our data favor a lighter component in the corresponding energy range. Our study demonstrates the potential of deep underground laboratories to provide new experimental insights into air shower physics and cosmic rays.

arxiv.org/abs/2512.21234.title: Gravitational open effective field theory of inflation
arxiv.org/abs/2512.21234.excerpt:
arXiv:2512.21234v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We construct a gravitational open extension of the effective field theory of inflation in the Schwinger-Keldysh framework. While physical symmetries allow many open operators in the Schwinger-Keldysh action, most of them overconstrain the equations of motion, yielding inconsistent dynamics. We identify a minimal open operator compatible with propagating scalar and tensor modes and build a local gravitational action, recovering known dissipative models of inflation.

arxiv.org/abs/2512.23730.title: Pair Space Analysis of Some Four-Body Central Configurations
arxiv.org/abs/2512.23730.excerpt:
arXiv:2512.23730v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: I study central configurations in the four-body problem, i.e., configurations in which the forces on all the bodies point to a fixed, single point in space. The newly formulated pair-space formalism yields a set of vectorial equations that fully characterize such configurations. I investigate a sub-class of solutions in which at least two pairs of inter-body distances are equal. The only such non-collinear configurations are the tetrahedron (the unique non-planar configuration), kites and the isosceles trapezium. The specific shapes (internal angles) are determined by the ratio of the masses of the bodies. Mathematical expressions are given for all these relations.

arxiv.org/abs/2602.04951.title: Impact on Inferred Neutron Star Equation of State due to Nonlinear Hydrodynamics, Background Spin, and Relativity
arxiv.org/abs/2602.04951.excerpt:
arXiv:2602.04951v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Tidal interaction is a unique, detectable signature in gravitational wave signals from inspiraling binary neutron stars (BNSs), which can be used to constrain the neutron star (NS) equation of state (EoS). The tidal interaction is resonantly amplified as the orbital frequency approaches the NS fundamental mode (f-mode) frequency. It has been shown that the exclusion of tidal resonance in parameter estimation leads to a significant bias in the inferred NS tidal deformability and hence the NS EoS [Pratten et al. PRL 129, 081102 (2022)]. The strength and location of tidal resonance depend sensitively on the f-mode frequency, which is typically modeled using its universal relation with the tidal deformability that is derived for an isolated, non-spinning NS assuming only linear fluid perturbations. In a BNS inspiral, the f-mode frequency can be corrected by at least three known effects: nonlinear hydrodynamics, background spin, and relativity. We use Hamiltonian Monte Carlo simulations to estimate the systematic bias on tidal deformability when each frequency correction is ignored. Our study considers both loud, individual events and the stacking of a population of detections. Both scenarios are expected when the next-generation detectors are available with a sensitivity level increased by about an order of magnitude.

arxiv.org/abs/2603.02652.title: Weinberg Angle, Neutron Abundance in BBN, and Lifetime
arxiv.org/abs/2603.02652.excerpt:
arXiv:2603.02652v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We present state of the art kinetic theory determination of the neutron abundance available for the Big-Bang nucleosynthesis (BBN). Our work is motivated by the study of the neutron lifespan measured in the laboratory and the unknown strength of weak interactions coupling constant $G_\mathrm{F}$ at finite temperature in the primordial Universe. We draw attention to the relevant dependence of $G_\mathrm{F}$ on the symmetry breaking Weinberg angle $s^2_\mathrm{W}$, a free parameter in the standard model of particle physics. We establish how the value of $s^2_\mathrm{W}$ by way of $G_\mathrm{F}$ modification influences neutron abundance available for BBN and neutron lifetime.

arxiv.org/abs/2603.28689.title: Probing soft signals of gravitational-wave memory with space-based interferometers
arxiv.org/abs/2603.28689.excerpt:
arXiv:2603.28689v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Gravitational-wave displacement memory is a remarkable, ubiquitous prediction of general relativity that has not yet been detected. Unlike the oscillatory components of gravitational waveforms, displacement memory is associated with soft gravitons and provides the leading low-frequency observable of its parent event. Analogous soft signals may also be associated with velocity and integrated-displacement memory. The simple, universal spectral shapes of soft waveforms provide effective templates for matched filtering and parameter estimation. In this paper, we investigate the detection prospects for such soft memory signals with future space-based laser interferometers. As realistic examples, we examine the infrared spectral features of gravitational waves from moderately relativistic nonspinning compact binary scattering and comparable-mass quasicircular, nonprecessing black hole mergers. In both cases, the low-frequency spectrum can be described by a soft displacement-memory waveform with finite-frequency corrections. Using the adopted instrumental-noise models, simulated Bayesian parameter-estimation analyses show that a single LISA-like detector can constrain the memory amplitude and arrival time for signals with matched-filter signal-to-noise ratios of order 10. Big Bang Observer (BBO) Stage 1 could measure null displacement memory from sufficiently loud stellar-mass compact binary mergers. We also evaluate the detectability of an idealized stochastic background of soft displacement-memory signals. These results establish gravitational-wave bursts with memory as concrete targets for space-based interferometers.

arxiv.org/abs/2606.17132.title: Are neutrinos Majorana? Fixed-target and high-energy astrophysical searches decide
arxiv.org/abs/2606.17132.excerpt:
arXiv:2606.17132v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The original version of this paper proposed a new approach to determining whether neutrinos are Dirac or Majorana fermions, a fundamental open question in particle physics. Conventional searches rely on neutrinoless double beta decay, but this electron-only channel suffers from blind spots. We propose a new, complementary probe to overcome this limitation. A heavy neutral lepton (HNL) triggers a high-energy shift in how the active neutrino flavors ($
u_e$, $
u_\mu$, $
u_	au$) mix---but only if the neutrinos are Majorana. For GeV-scale HNLs, the upcoming beam-dump experiment SHiP can discover the HNL and measure how it mixes with the active flavors. However, the proposed signature of the Majorana nature of neutrinos does not exist. The reasons are explained here. The analysis has been superseded by Ref.~\cite{Barenboim:2026udr}. The original version is retained as v1 for the record.

arxiv.org/abs/2606.23787.title: Multi-peaked high-frequency gravitational waves from PBH-assisted leptogenesis
arxiv.org/abs/2606.23787.excerpt:
arXiv:2606.23787v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We study the possibility of probing non-thermal leptogenesis with multi-peaked high-frequency gravitational waves (GW) by considering heavy right-handed neutrino (RHN) produced from primordial black hole (PBH) evaporation to be responsible for generating the required lepton asymmetry. The decay of RHN also produces a GW spectrum due to graviton bremsstrahlung with the corresponding amplitude being enhanced for heavier RHN. The presence of an ultra-light PBH dominated epoch not only ensures sufficient production of RHNs, but also keeps the leptogenesis scenario free from strong washout problem of thermal leptogenesis at very high scale. In addition, the PBH dominated epoch also helps in generating a gravitational bremsstrahlung spectrum distinct from the stochastic GW background from the thermal bath. Finally, PBH evaporation also brings two separate sources of GW via density perturbation and graviton emission via Hawking evaporation. For the most optimistic scenario with very high scale seesaw consistent with neutrino mass and leptogenesis, this leads to a multi-peaked GW spectrum with peak frequencies lying in the MHz-EHz range.

arxiv.org/abs/2608.13206.title: Long-term 3+1 simulations of primordial black hole formation during radiation domination
arxiv.org/abs/2608.13206.excerpt:
arXiv:2608.13206v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We develop an efficient three-dimensional numerical-relativity framework for primordial black-hole (PBH) formation from superhorizon curvature perturbations in a radiation-dominated Universe. We implement flux-conservative relativistic hydrodynamics in the adaptive-mesh-refinement code GRChombo and introduce a cosmologically scaled Gamma-driver that allows the cosmic-time step to grow in proportion to the scale factor. For a representative long-term simulation, the scaled driver preserves the apparent-horizon mass evolution and constraint behavior while reducing the number of coarse-level advances by a factor of approximately $94$ relative to the standard driver. We also construct a conformal-time version of the moving-puncture gauge as a consistency check. Applying the framework to a spherical Gaussian curvature profile, we find a collapse threshold $\mu_c \simeq 0.7958$ and approximate critical mass scaling, consistent with previous spherically symmetric results. We further fit the late-time PBH mass growth to the Zel'dovich--Novikov accretion law, demonstrating that the code can follow both near-critical collapse and long-term post-formation evolution in three dimensions. The framework provides a foundation for future studies of PBH formation beyond spherical symmetry.

arxiv.org/abs/2609.00157.title: Magnetic field-induced enhancement and quenching of Urca emission in quark matter
arxiv.org/abs/2609.00157.excerpt:
arXiv:2609.00157v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Using first-principles field-theoretic methods, we investigate neutrino emission from strongly magnetized dense quark matter under conditions relevant to compact stars. We account for Landau-level quantization of both electron and quark states and show that it strongly modifies the kinematics of Urca processes. In particular, quark quantization restricts the available phase space in which both quark and electron energies can simultaneously lie near their respective Fermi surfaces. At moderately strong magnetic fields, before pronounced quark quantization sets in, the emission rate tends to increase on average with increasing field strength. In the regime of very strong fields, however, the increasingly restricted phase space first gives rise to Shubnikov--de Haas-type oscillations and then to resonance-like spikes near a discrete sequence of Urca-resonant magnetic field values, separated by regions of strong suppression. Finally, the emission rate becomes nearly completely quenched once $|eB| \gtrsim 6\mu_{e}\mu_{u}$, corresponding to approximately $B\gtrsim 1.5\times 10^{19}~\mbox{G}$ for the representative set of model parameters considered. We also find significant anisotropy in the longitudinal momentum emission near the Urca-resonant magnetic field values.

arxiv.org/abs/2609.17412.title: Cosmological Constrained Axion-Portal Inelastic Dark Matter for the LZ Event
arxiv.org/abs/2609.17412.excerpt:
arXiv:2609.17412v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The recent high-recoil candidate event reported by LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) motivates dark-matter scenarios with nonstandard kinematics and momentum-dependent interactions. We study a two-state inelastic dark-matter model in which $\chi_1$ and $\chi_2$ couple off-diagonally to an axion-like particle (ALP) that also couples to gluons and photons. Unlike treatments that assume only one dark-matter state is present today, we track the cosmological evolution of both states. The excited state $\chi_2$ is sufficiently long-lived to survive to the present, with its relic fraction determined by the dark-sector conversion process $\chi_2\chi_2\leftrightarrow\chi_1\chi_1$. We find that this fraction depends strongly on the Lorentz structure of the DM--ALP interaction. Scalar transition couplings lead to nonperturbative conversion rates with a pronounced resonant structure, yielding a final excited-state fraction that varies nonmonotonically with the mediator mass, from $f_2\sim10^{-4}$ to approximately $1/2$ over the parameter range studied. The relative importance of endothermic and exothermic scattering is therefore parameter dependent. By contrast, pseudoscalar transition couplings preserve $f_2\simeq1/2$, yielding recoil spectra dominated by exothermic $\chi_2 N\to\chi_1 N$ down-scattering for the benchmarks considered. Benchmark spectra in all four scenarios can peak near the observed recoil energy of $250\,\mathrm{keV}$. Our results demonstrate that the dominant direction of inelastic scattering in direct detection can be dynamically selected by the early-Universe evolution of the dark sector. With additional data, annual modulation measurements could distinguish these scenarios. We further show that the ALP portal can be directly probed at colliders.

arxiv.org/abs/2609.38316.title: Constraints on Complex Electroweak WIMPs from Solar Capture
arxiv.org/abs/2609.38316.excerpt:
arXiv:2609.38316v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: One of the most convincing realizations of particle dark matter is provided by models based on electroweak multiplets. The lightest neutral state of such a multiplet can be a stable Majorana fermion or a real scalar, and its phenomenology is governed by two parameters: the dark matter mass and the mass splitting $\{m_\chi,\delta\}$. The sub-MeV range for $\delta$ is particularly important as it allows for a large inelastic scattering cross section. In this paper, we analyze solar capture, energy loss, and annihilation of scalar and fermionic electroweak multiplet dark matter, generalizing earlier results for the Higgsino to other representations. We find that, while the case of a doublet is somewhat special, higher representations behave in a self-similar way. For the higher multiplets, IceCube results constrain the splitting to $\delta \gtrsim 350$ keV for all dark matter masses up to $100$ TeV. Assuming thermal freeze-out and a Standard Halo Model velocity distribution, this rules out most models of electroweak dark matter as a possible origin of the single high-recoil event reported by the LZ collaboration. We also show that a high-velocity tail in the dark matter distribution, such as that induced by the Large Magellanic Cloud, raises the splitting preferred by the LZ event above the solar bounds for many of the multiplets.

arxiv.org/abs/2610.41082.title: Two-Fluid Radial Stability of Dark-Matter-Admixed Compact Objects: Dark Compact Planets, Dark White Dwarfs, Dark Neutron Stars, and Dark Oysters
arxiv.org/abs/2610.41082.excerpt:
arXiv:2610.41082v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We investigate the equilibrium structure and stability against radial oscillations of a variety of two-fluid compact objects containing ordinary baryonic matter admixed with cold dark matter coupled through the background spacetime. For the ordinary fluid, we employ a QCD equation of state compatible with chiral effective field theory at nuclear densities (supplemented by the BPS and Negele-Vautherin models at extremely low densities) and with perturbative QCD in the high-density regime while also satisfying also current astrophysical data. For the dark fluid, we assume self-interacting fermionic matter with particle masses of $m_f=$ 2, 5, 10, and 100 GeV and two self-interaction strengths of $y=0.1$ and $10^3$. By scanning a large range of central pressures for both fluids, we identify the presence of dark compact planets, dark white dwarfs, dark neutron stars and the so-called dark oysters. Importantly, these objects are not only in two-fluid hydrostatic equilibrium, but they are also stable against two-fluid radial oscillations. We find that the relative representation of each class in the radially stable sample is strongly sensitive to the combinations of $m_f$ and $y$, with some combinations entirely suppressing some of these object classes within the sampled domain while favoring others. In addition to these classes, strong self-repulsion supports stable, dark-matter-dominated branches with compact ordinary-matter cores and extended dark halos, approaching the self-interacting fermion-star limit. Finally, we calculate the gravitational redshift at the ordinary-matter surface, $z_{\rm OM}$, including the contribution of extended dark-matter halos for which we found radially stable configurations with $z_{\rm OM}>2$.

phys.org/news/2026-11-science-scientists.title: What is science? Even scientists can't agree
phys.org/news/2026-11-science-scientists.excerpt: Scientists spend their careers trying to understand the world, but a new study suggests they have surprisingly different ideas about what science itself is. The study, published in Royal Society Open Science, found that scientists disagree about the meaning and purpose of science even more than the general public does. Of the 18 descriptions of science examined, few received unqualified endorsement from scientists, who often expressed reservations even about ideas they generally agreed with.

phys.org/news/2026-11-asteroid-platinum-.title: Asteroid mining will crash the platinum market, but that's good news for Earth
phys.org/news/2026-11-asteroid-platinum-.excerpt: Science fiction authors have been dreaming of robotic spacecraft harvesting fortunes from asteroids for decades. Humanity is slowly getting closer to that reality. But if you ask asteroid mining skeptics, they will usually ask one specific question—what happens to the prices of all those rare materials once someone actually brings them back? A pair of system dynamicists from MIT directly tackled that question with a new paper titled Will AstroForge Collapse the PGM Market?

phys.org/news/2026-11-lingering-blue-une.title: A lingering blue glow and unexpected energy levels hint at new ways to control light in advanced materials
phys.org/news/2026-11-lingering-blue-une.excerpt: Scientists from the Physics Department and Organic Electroactive Materials research group at Durham University have made significant advances in understanding how materials absorb and release light in two recently published research papers in Nature Communications.

phys.org/news/2026-11-scientists-wild-he.title: Scientists find some of the 'very last wild and healthy ecosystems' in the world's oceans untouched by humans
phys.org/news/2026-11-scientists-wild-he.excerpt: Humans have left their mark on virtually every place on the planet, from the deep sea to the peaks of the highest mountains. But a few very remote atolls in the Pacific Ocean may be exceptions. A new Frontiers in Marine Science study has found two coral atolls, Bikar and Bokak, located on the territory of the Marshall Islands, to be some of the most intact ecosystems remaining in the region and perhaps the world.

phys.org/news/2026-11-iberian-season-lar.title: Record-breaking 2025 Iberian fire season was three times larger due to climate change
phys.org/news/2026-11-iberian-season-lar.excerpt: The latest global State of Wildfires report, co-led by the University of East Anglia, shows that the extreme fire-prone weather experienced across Spain and Portugal in 2025 was three times more likely due to human-caused climate change, and the area burned was three times larger. The paper is published in Earth System Science Data.

phys.org/news/2026-11-humility-social-we.title: Living with humility took on social weight in the late Middle Ages, historian argues
phys.org/news/2026-11-humility-social-we.excerpt: We're deep in the Middle Ages. In the mind's eye, monks stagger past, flagellating themselves to cleanse their sins and demonstrate their humility before God and creation. This was a time when humility—humilitas—was considered one of the fundamental virtues of Christian life.

phys.org/news/2026-11-important-tropical.title: More important than tropical cyclones: Scientists finally track the hidden weather systems behind most tropical rainfall
phys.org/news/2026-11-important-tropical.excerpt: For the first time, researchers in Australia have identified and tracked the weather systems that are collectively more important to rainfall across the tropics than tropical cyclones. The work, published in the journal Weather and Climate Dynamics, has advanced a new way to investigate how tropical rain may change as the Earth warms up.

phys.org/news/2026-11-pipes-status-18th-.title: How pipes became status symbols in 18th-century Sweden
phys.org/news/2026-11-pipes-status-18th-.excerpt: In the 18th century, a clay tobacco pipe could reveal more than you might think. Its length, quality and condition, as well as the way it was used, could signal social status. In a new doctoral thesis, Lund University archaeologist Robert Bergman Carter shows how smokeways at the time served as clear markers of status.

phys.org/news/2026-11-loyal-donors-advic.title: Why holding on to loyal donors is not the right advice for every nonprofit
phys.org/news/2026-11-loyal-donors-advic.excerpt: As humanitarian funding shrinks, conventional fundraising wisdom says to hold on to loyal donors. But new research shows that the value of a donor depends on how a nonprofit is set up. For many organizations, winning new donors matters more than keeping loyal ones.

phys.org/news/2026-11-similar-cloud-clim.title: Why similar changes in cloud cover can have different climate effects
phys.org/news/2026-11-similar-cloud-clim.excerpt: Marine low clouds over the world's eastern subtropical oceans strongly influence Earth's temperature by reflecting sunlight back to space. How these clouds change as the planet warms is one of the biggest uncertainties in predicting the severity of future warming.

phys.org/news/2026-11-deep-sea-mollusk-h.title: Deep-sea mollusk houses bacteria in tiny 'dragon balls,' revealing a new symbiotic structure
phys.org/news/2026-11-deep-sea-mollusk-h.excerpt: Researchers at The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) have discovered a previously unknown specialized organelle structure in a deep-sea mollusk living at cold seeps in the South China Sea. Dedicated to maintaining bacterial symbiosis, this newly identified survival mechanism provides new insights into how deep-sea organisms adapt to nearly oxygen-free environments and opens new directions for research on chemosymbiosis, organelle evolution and deep-sea ecosystems.

phys.org/news/2026-11-method-dna-epigene.title: New method maps DNA folding and epigenetic marks in single cells
phys.org/news/2026-11-method-dna-epigene.excerpt: A new experimental procedure developed by researchers at Yale School of Medicine could help scientists better understand how DNA structure influences disease and development.

phys.org/news/2026-11-drylands-microbes-.title: When rain finally does come to drylands, only some microbes in the soil 'awaken'
phys.org/news/2026-11-drylands-microbes-.excerpt: In arid regions, the microbes that power threatened dryland soil ecosystems called biological soil crusts stay dormant over long periods, only "awakening" when they sense moisture from infrequent rainfall. Now, a team led by researchers at Penn State—driven by projections that those biocrusts will decline by as much as 40% in the next 45 years—found that when a dryland soil does get wet, most of the microbes in the biocrust stay inactive. It's a discovery that will inform ongoing efforts to conserve and restore biocrusts, according to the researchers.

phys.org/news/2026-11-biologists-reveal-.title: Biologists reveal chlorophyll-building enzyme's structure for first time and clarify its mechanism
phys.org/news/2026-11-biologists-reveal-.excerpt: Plants are green because of a pigment that is key to photosynthesis: chlorophyll. In its production, the enzyme chlorophyll synthase plays an important role. As part of an international collaboration, researchers from Osnabrück University, the Center Algatech in Třeboň and the University of Sheffield have now succeeded in deciphering the structure of this enzyme and gaining valuable insights into its mechanism. The findings are published in the journal Nature Chemical Biology.

phys.org/news/2026-11-biodegradable-lact.title: Biodegradable bubble moves away from lactic acid without a motor—a step toward artificial cells
phys.org/news/2026-11-biodegradable-lact.excerpt: A tiny biodegradable bubble can move away from a chemical on its own, without a motor. Living cells need complex molecular machinery to do this. This discovery by researchers led by chemist Daniela Wilson at Radboud University, together with colleagues at Durham University, is a step toward artificial cells with lifelike behavior and could, in the long term, provide an interesting approach for self-steering particles in targeted drug delivery.

phys.org/news/2026-11-scientists-extinct.title: Scientists challenge the dream of bringing extinct species back to life
phys.org/news/2026-11-scientists-extinct.excerpt: Could extinction itself become a thing of the past? Advances in biotechnology, including ancient DNA sequencing, genome analysis and gene editing, have led some to believe that it may be possible to bring extinct species back to life.

phys.org/news/2026-11-chip-cells-electri.title: Chip identifies cells by their electrical signature, then separates them with a precisely aimed sound wave
phys.org/news/2026-11-chip-cells-electri.excerpt: In biomedicine, sorting cells accurately without damaging them remains a persistent problem. Current methods, like fluorescence-activated cell sorting, rely on labeling the cells extrinsically, which can stress the cells, alter their behavior and even interfere with the assay. A collaborative study between researchers in Singapore and China has now developed a noninvasive, label-free method to sort cells.

phys.org/news/2026-11-remedy-proactive-a.title: From remedy to prevention: Researchers call for proactive approach to protect the human right to water
phys.org/news/2026-11-remedy-proactive-a.excerpt: More than 2 billion people, or approximately one-quarter of the world's population, lack access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene, according to the United Nations Children's Fund. Today, 16 years after the U.N. General Assembly recognized this access as a fundamental human right, its legal protection is well established, but the reality on the ground lags behind.

phys.org/news/2026-11-clay-figurines-pre.title: Symbolic clay figurines change our understanding of the prehistoric Middle East
phys.org/news/2026-11-clay-figurines-pre.excerpt: Newly discovered artifacts are evidence of the earliest known example of a tradition of making clay figurines in the Middle East—and challenge long-held beliefs about when and how clay began to be used for symbolic purposes in the region, according to a study published in PLOS One by Laurent Davin from The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Israel, and colleagues.

phys.org/news/2026-11-monkey-foot-palm-d.title: Monkey foot and palm prints differ between individuals, as they do in humans
phys.org/news/2026-11-monkey-foot-palm-d.excerpt: In three species of monkey, the complex pattern of ridges on the feet and palms varies between individuals, similar to human fingerprints, according to a study published in the open-access journal PLOS One by Juliana Vieira Flores Sales at Universidade de Brasília and colleagues.

phys.org/news/2026-11-statistics-common-.title: Misunderstandings about statistics common even among experienced researchers
phys.org/news/2026-11-statistics-common-.excerpt: Even researchers and people with extensive training in statistics often find it difficult to interpret statistical results correctly. This is shown by a new systematic review carried out by Uppsala University and others, in which researchers have analyzed 55 studies involving over 15,000 participants. The work is published in PLOS One.

phys.org/news/2026-11-spain-massive-ston.title: Spain's massive stone tombs reveal collective burials continued well into Bronze Age
phys.org/news/2026-11-spain-massive-ston.excerpt: Iberian people continued using, and possibly building, massive necropolises well into the Bronze Age, according to a study published in PLOS One by Eduardo Vijande-Vila of the University of Cádiz, Spain, and colleagues.

phys.org/news/2026-11-frozen-sperm-enabl.title: Frozen sperm enables embryo development in endangered Japanese bird for first time—but chick fails to hatch
phys.org/news/2026-11-frozen-sperm-enabl.excerpt: The Okinawa rail (Hypotaenidia okinawae) is an endangered flightless bird endemic to the Yanbaru forest region of Okinawa Island in Japan. The bird has only recently begun recovering its numbers after introduced predators, such as the mongoose, and traffic accidents reduced its population to as low as 820 individuals.

phys.org/news/2026-11-overheating-cattle.title: Overheating cattle: More and more dangerous heat is coming for northern Australia's herds
phys.org/news/2026-11-overheating-cattle.excerpt: The Sunday roast and the backyard barbecue have long been Australian rituals. The country is one of the world's biggest consumers of red meat. The average Australian ate about 22 kilograms (49 pounds) of beef in 2024.

phys.org/news/2026-11-excess-reliance-ai.title: Excess reliance on AI could harm independent thinking in humanities education
phys.org/news/2026-11-excess-reliance-ai.excerpt: The increasing use of content generated using artificial intelligence (AI) tools in university humanities classrooms is challenging what we think of as traditional academic integrity, intellectual responsibility and the authority of teachers, according to research in the International Journal of Innovation and Sustainable Development.

phys.org/news/2026-11-ancient-dna-reveal.title: Ancient DNA reveals rare genetic condition behind a 1,600-year-old infant's single eye socket
phys.org/news/2026-11-ancient-dna-reveal.excerpt: Cyclopia is the most severe form of a rare birth condition in which the developing brain fails to divide into two separate halves. This can also affect facial development, sometimes leaving the baby with a single eye socket in the center of the forehead and severe facial abnormalities. Most babies born with this condition either die before or soon after birth. It is so rare that it occurs in roughly 1 in 100,000 births, so finding physical evidence of it from modern times is difficult, let alone from historical ones.

phys.org/news/2026-11-defense-photosynth.title: A double defense protects photosynthesis from extreme heat
phys.org/news/2026-11-defense-photosynth.excerpt: Photosynthesis is fundamental to life on Earth, allowing plants and microalgae to convert sunlight and carbon dioxide into organic compounds. However, this essential process is highly vulnerable to heat. As global temperatures rise and heat waves become more frequent, declining photosynthetic efficiency threatens agricultural productivity and the large-scale cultivation of microalgae for biofuels and other valuable products.

phys.org/news/2026-11-3d-protein-complex.title: 3D protein complex model sheds light on barley grain dormancy
phys.org/news/2026-11-3d-protein-complex.excerpt: Researchers from Adelaide University and Plant Synthetic Biology Australia have uncovered new insights into the molecular machinery controlling the dormancy-to-germination transition in barley, potentially paving the way for improved crop varieties and better outcomes for farmers, maltsters and brewers.

phys.org/news/2026-11-account-role-negle.title: Taking into account the role of neglected farmer groups in recharging groundwater
phys.org/news/2026-11-account-role-negle.excerpt: A new study by researchers at the Indo-French Cell for Water Sciences (IFCWS), Indian Institute of Science (IISc), introduces a new framework for water budgeting in agricultural regions that includes farmers' social categories that are usually neglected. The work is published in the Journal of Hydrology.

phys.org/news/2026-11-centaurus-spotligh.title: Centaurus A in the spotlight: Plasma simulations reproduce black hole jets' mysterious bright edges
phys.org/news/2026-11-centaurus-spotligh.excerpt: Around 12 million light-years away, the supermassive black hole of the galaxy Centaurus A is hurling two enormous plasma jets into space at nearly the speed of light. These so-called jets are brighter at their edges than at their center. The reason for this was previously unclear but has now been explained by a team from the Chair of Astronomy at the University of Würzburg. The research is published in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.

space.com/space-exploration/launches-spa.excerpt: Rocket Lab has raised the launch cost of its next-gen Neutron rocket by more than 25%, an increase that reflects high demand amid a looming liftoff bottleneck.

astronomy.com/observing/zwo-introduces-t.title: ZWO introduces the Seestar S30 Plus
astronomy.com/observing/zwo-introduces-t.excerpt: ZWO has added a new entry point to its smart telescope lineup. The Seestar S30 Plus went on sale Nov. 10 for $499 — $474 for a limited time — undercutting the S30 Pro by $200 and making it the cheapest Seestar available. “Many people are interested in astrophotography but hesitate when they see the Continue reading "ZWO introduces the Seestar S30 Plus" The post ZWO introduces the Seestar S30 Plus appeared first on Astronomy Magazine .

universetoday.com/articles/the-ice-giant.title: The Ice Giants' Magnetic Fields are Very Strange Compared to Earth's
universetoday.com/articles/the-ice-giant.excerpt: Uranus and Neptune, the Solar System's ice giants, have interiors unlike the other planets. As a result, they also have magnetic fields unlike the others. They're messy and tilted, and Voyager 2, the only spacecraft to even flyby them, showed us how messy they are. New research uses models to try to understand what's going on with the pair of planets and their weird fields, and found that it's likely they change on very short timescales. They could already be much different than when Voyager 2 visited in the late 1980s.

universetoday.com/articles/asteroid-mini.title: Asteroid Mining Will Crash the Platinum Market, But That’s Good News for Earth
universetoday.com/articles/asteroid-mini.excerpt: Science fiction authors have been dreaming of robotic spacecraft harvesting fortunes from asteroids for decades. Humanity is slowly getting closer to that reality. But if you ask asteroid mining skeptics, they will usually ask one specific question - what happens to the prices of all those rare materials once someone actually brings them back? A pair of system dynamicists from MIT directly tackled that question with a new paper titled Will AstroForge Collapse the PGM Market?

universetoday.com/articles/the-chandra-x.title: The Chandra X-Ray Observatory Unmasks a Supernova Impostor
universetoday.com/articles/the-chandra-x.excerpt: Some stars, called Luminous Blue Variables, can be confused with supernovae explosions. They exhibit similar outbursts, but unlike supernovae, which explode once and then are gone forever, these stars have periodic outbursts. New research found that one of these 'supernova impostors' is in a binary relationship with a black hole or a neutron star, and that explains its periodic outbursts.

newscientist.com/article/2598571-some-pf.title: Some PFAS chemicals are declining in English rivers but others are appearing
newscientist.com/article/2598571-some-pf.excerpt: The levels of two globally restricted "forever chemicals" linked to health issues are showing a strong downwards trend in English rivers, but their understudied replacements are starting to fill the gap

phys.org/news/2026-11-romania-kazakhstan.title: From Romania to Kazakhstan, summer droughts linked to less winter ice in two rapidly warming seas
phys.org/news/2026-11-romania-kazakhstan.excerpt: This summer, with its scarce rainfall and repeated heat waves, witnessed one of the most severe droughts in Europe since 1540. The resulting wildfires across western Europe received considerable media attention, but eastern Europe was also heavily hit, worsening the humanitarian crisis caused by the war in Ukraine. Simulations have shown that such droughts are bound to become more frequent and severe in the future due to man-made global warming.

phys.org/news/2026-11-war-world-years.ht.title: How war has connected the world for 500 years
phys.org/news/2026-11-war-world-years.ht.excerpt: With wars raging in Ukraine and across the Middle East, commentators increasingly ask whether we're sliding toward a third world war. But what makes a war "global"?

phys.org/news/2026-11-indonesia-million-.title: Indonesia fires burned through nearly 2.9 million hectares: Monitor
phys.org/news/2026-11-indonesia-million-.excerpt: Fires in Indonesia driven partly by a strong El Niño have burned through 2.88 million hectares (7.1 million acres) so far in 2026, a monitor analyzing satellite imagery told AFP on Wednesday.

phys.org/news/2026-11-england-young-work.title: Only half of England's young workers outside higher education secure permanent contracts, down from 81%
phys.org/news/2026-11-england-young-work.excerpt: The study of young people in England found that among those who did not progress to higher education, only 16% secured apprenticeships and just 23% had secured stable work by ages 19–20. Of those in work, only half had a permanent contract, down from 81% in a similar study six years ago.

phys.org/news/2026-11-ocean-liner-larges.title: Retired ocean liner to become largest artificial reef in the world
phys.org/news/2026-11-ocean-liner-larges.excerpt: Bigger than the RMS Titanic and faster than the RMS Queen Mary, the SS United States was a nautical wonder during the mid-20th century—the nation's premier luxury ocean liner that once ferried presidents and Hollywood elite across the Atlantic in opulence.

phys.org/news/2026-11-microplastics-wild.title: Microplastics found in wild mammals' blood more than 40 miles from human infrastructure
phys.org/news/2026-11-microplastics-wild.excerpt: Animals, like humans, are taking up increasing amounts of tiny plastic particles. Such microplastics are demonstrably hazardous to many species under experimental conditions, and it is suspected that they may also pose a threat to animals in the wild. While data about microplastic concentrations in the terrestrial environment exist, it has not yet been clear if higher exposure also translates into higher microplastic accumulation in individual animals. A new paper published in Nature now confirms this link.

phys.org/news/2026-11-genetic-landscape-.title: New study maps the genetic landscape of bovine TB across Wales
phys.org/news/2026-11-genetic-landscape-.excerpt: Bovine tuberculosis is evolving in different ways across different regions in Wales, according to the most detailed analysis of the bacterium conducted to date. One of the most significant animal health challenges facing Wales, bovine TB affects cattle health and farm businesses and places considerable emotional, social and financial pressures on farming communities.

phys.org/news/2026-11-parasites-fungus-i.title: Even parasites have parasites: Fungus infects powdery mildew
phys.org/news/2026-11-parasites-fungus-i.excerpt: In the fungal kingdom, no one is safe from parasites—not even other parasites. A new study from North Carolina State University finds that Ampelomyces, an intracellular fungus that infects the plant disease powdery mildew, is far more common than previously known. By screening museum samples of powdery mildews up to about 150 years old, researchers discovered that not only is Ampelomyces quite common, but many specimens labeled as Ampelomyces are misidentified.

phys.org/news/2026-11-independent-techni.title: Independent technique validates landmark M87* image
phys.org/news/2026-11-independent-techni.excerpt: The 2019 Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) image was the work of hundreds of scientists and captured the first direct view of a black hole's shadow—becoming one of the most recognized scientific images of the modern era. A team of four from CSIRO, Australia's national science agency, has developed a powerful new imaging technique that validated the landmark 2019 image of the black hole at the center of galaxy M87.

phys.org/news/2026-11-hidden-technology-.title: Clean water, hidden risks: New technology reveals neurotoxicity missed by conventional water quality monitoring
phys.org/news/2026-11-hidden-technology-.excerpt: A photograph of an orchestra can tell you whether the musicians are on stage and their instruments are intact. But it cannot tell you whether they are playing in harmony. Even when every musician is present, a subtle loss of coordination can change the entire performance.

phys.org/news/2026-11-fluorescent-probes.title: Fluorescent probes reveal fluid-like barriers inside nuclear pores of living human cells
phys.org/news/2026-11-fluorescent-probes.excerpt: Our genetic material is hidden inside the nucleus of our cells, well protected by a double membrane. All molecules wishing to pass through must thread their way through one of several thousand nuclear pores. The scaffold structure of these pores is well known. However, exactly how transport takes place within them has been the subject of much debate. Researchers at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (JGU), the Max Planck Institute for Biophysics (MPI-BP) in Frankfurt am Main and Wuhan University in China have now shed light on the matter.

phys.org/news/2026-11-superconducting-vo.title: Superconducting vortices provide experimental evidence that clogging is a phase transition
phys.org/news/2026-11-superconducting-vo.excerpt: Clogging is a phenomenon in which moving particles get stuck, slowing or blocking the flow, but how this transition occurs has remained experimentally unproven. Researchers from Science Tokyo studied superconducting vortices to demonstrate that clogging is a nonequilibrium phase transition. Using a two-step measurement protocol, they distinguished clogging from conventional pinning and revealed that both transitions share a critical point, offering new insights into predicting and controlling clogging across diverse systems.

phys.org/news/2026-11-lurks-newfoundland.title: What lurks 'Below' Newfoundland waters? A marine biologist explains the science behind the show
phys.org/news/2026-11-lurks-newfoundland.excerpt: When I learned that Netflix planned to film the miniseries Below, about a sea monster terrorizing a Newfoundland outport, I thought to myself: "THIS I've gotta see!"

phys.org/news/2026-11-looping-dna-nectar.title: Looping DNA may help flowers grow nectar-producing organs
phys.org/news/2026-11-looping-dna-nectar.excerpt: Nectaries are specialized floral tissues that secrete nectar to attract pollinators. Although the protein CRABS CLAW (CRC) is established as essential for nectary formation, the exact molecular mechanisms governing how it drives organ growth and secretion have remained unknown.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261110.title: A massive new simulation reveals how the universe emerged from darkness
sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261110.excerpt: A groundbreaking new supercomputer simulation is revealing how the universe escaped its cosmic dark age and transformed into a cosmos filled with stars and galaxies. Called Lumina, it recreates 2 billion years of early cosmic history across a region 1.6 billion light-years wide, capturing extraordinary details that previous simulations could not.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261109.title: NASA’s Parker Solar Probe discovers a hidden pattern in the Sun’s chaotic magnetic fields
sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261109.excerpt: NASA’s Parker Solar Probe has revealed a surprising secret hidden within the chaos of space: turbulent magnetic fields reverse their direction of rotation when examined at extremely small scales. The discovery exposes an unexpected pattern in solar wind turbulence that could help scientists better understand solar activity and predict geomagnetic storms.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261108.title: Scientists discover that necks didn't evolve for the reason we thought
sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261108.excerpt: Scientists have discovered that the first animals to venture onto land nearly 380 million years ago had surprisingly stiff necks, overturning a long-standing theory about evolution. Rather than evolving to help animals turn their heads, necks may have emerged as part of the anatomical changes that allowed them to move using their front limbs.

sciencealert.com/a-single-nuclear-explos.title: Study Shows a Single Nuclear Blast Could Disable 99% of Satellites in a Matter of Days
sciencealert.com/a-single-nuclear-explos.excerpt: Utterly devastating. ScienceAlert stories are written, fact-checked, and edited by humans, never generated by AI. Don't miss a story, subscribe here.

insideclimatenews.org/news/11112026/cact.title: Even Cacti Are Threatened by Heat and Drought From Global Warming
insideclimatenews.org/news/11112026/cact.excerpt: Cacti are among the toughest plants on the planet, withstanding scorching temperatures and parched conditions that would wilt a more sensitive sprout. But climate change may threaten these hardy plants more than previously thought, a new study suggests.  Scientists in recent years have raised some concerns over the effects of rising temperatures on cactus species, […]

space.com/space-exploration/launches-spa.title: SpaceX launches 2nd mystery mission for US Space Force in 6-day span (photos)
space.com/space-exploration/launches-spa.excerpt: SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force from California tonight (Nov. 11), the second such mission for the company in a six-day span.

9.headline: Ultracold Rubidium Atoms Mimic Schwinger Pair Production
9.summary: Researchers used an optical lattice of ultracold rubidium atoms to simulate the elusive Schwinger effect, revealing how mass and field strength control pair creation.
highlights: Ultracold rubidium atoms were arranged in a one‑dimensional optical lattice to represent a false vacuum
Tuning the simulated particle mass and background electric field altered the observed pair‑production rate
Quantum gas microscope imaging captured real‑time dynamics of the simulated particle‑antiparticle creation

7.headline: Delayed Rise of Lyman Continuum Escape in Bursty High‑Redshift Galaxies
7.summary: Simulations show that Lyman continuum escape fractions peak about 16 Myr after star‑formation bursts, especially in massive early galaxies.
highlights: Typical LyC escape lag is ~16 Myr with peak correlations of 0.4‑0.6 in massive haloes
Delay scales as M★⁻⁰·¹⁹ and Mhalo⁻⁰·²⁷, lengthening for lower‑mass systems
Hα‑to‑UV luminosity ratio retains a delayed link to LyC escape, offering an observable tracer

15.headline: Astrolabe Surrogate Generates Full‑Resolution Cosmology Simulations via Flow Matching
15.summary: Astrolabe uses a flow‑matching transformer to emulate particle‑level cosmology, delivering accurate large‑scale structure without voxel resolution limits.
highlights: Acts directly on 6N phase‑space coordinates of individual particles
Employs a hybrid transformer where each particle cross‑attends to multiscale field tokens
Matches physical flow using approximate COLA coordinates, preserving momentum and mass
Reproduces power spectra, halo mass functions, velocity and density profiles in Lambda‑CDM tests
Generalizes to dark‑acoustic oscillation initial conditions and scales to TNG50‑3‑dark size

8.headline: Rare FN1 Mutation Shields APOE ε4 Carriers from Alzheimer’s Brain Damage
8.summary: Scientists identified a protective FN1 mutation that limits fibrotic buildup around brain vessels, preserving blood‑brain barrier integrity in APOE ε4 carriers into their 80s.
highlights: APOE ε4 drives excess fibronectin accumulation around cerebral blood vessels
A rare FN1 mutation reduces fibronectin deposition and prevents barrier leakage
Single‑cell and spatial analyses confirmed the mechanism in mouse, zebrafish, and human tissue
Findings published in Nature Aging suggest new therapeutic targets for early Alzheimer’s intervention

11.headline: JWST Spectroscopy Reveals Common Mini‑Quenched Galaxies at z > 4
11.summary: Deep 28‑hour NIRSpec/PRISM observations in the OASIS program find that suppressed, mini‑quenched and lulling galaxies constitute a sizable fraction of early low‑mass galaxies.
highlights: Three mini‑quenched galaxies with log(M/Msun)=8.3‑8.9 lie 1.2‑1.7 dex below the star‑forming main sequence
Five lulling galaxies show weak Balmer emission just above the quenching threshold
Suppressed galaxies represent 29% of the sample at z=4‑5.5, with a number density ≈1.6×10⁻³ Mpc⁻³ dex⁻¹
Photometric estimates overstate star‑formation rates, misclassifying most candidates without spectroscopy

12.headline: Mineral‑Forming Techniques Capture Over 99% of Technetium‑99 from Waste
12.summary: Researchers at the University of Manchester have shown that engineered minerals can lock more than 99% of radioactive Technetium‑99 from liquid waste into stable forms.
highlights: Layered double hydroxides incorporated Technetium‑99 into their octahedral layers, achieving >99% removal from solution.
Methylene diphosphonic acid formed a soluble Tc‑MDP complex captured by hydroxyapatite, removing up to 99% in flowing
Advanced X‑ray analysis at Diamond Light Source confirmed mineral incorporation, and microbes were shown to aid Tc‑MDP complex

6.headline: ALMA Detects Water, Methanol and Methyl Formate in HD 100546 and IRS 48 Disks
6.summary: ALMA band 5 observations reveal methanol‑rich IRS 48 with no water, while HD 100546 shows both water and methanol, yielding a comet‑like CH₃OH/H₂O ratio.
highlights: IRS 48 disk shows methanol detection but water vapor remains undetected, giving methanol‑to‑water column ratio >0.2.
HD 100546 disk contains water and methanol with CH₃OH/H₂O ≈0.02, matching the median cometary value.
Methyl formate‑to‑methanol ratio is ~0.2 in IRS 48 and ~2 in HD 100546, indicating chemical enhancement in the latter.
Non‑LTE analysis constrains optical depths and emitting regions of methanol lines in both disks.

4.headline: Chandra Reveals Kiloparsec-Scale Jet at Record-Breaking z=6.1
4.summary: Deep 360 ks Chandra observations resolve the distant AGN jet into two X‑ray components, showing a steep photon index and an 18% extended‑to‑core luminosity ratio.
highlights: Extended X‑ray emission splits into two slightly resolved components
Photon index of the jet is Γ = 2.25, steeper than the core’s Γ = 1.86
Extended‑to‑core luminosity ratio reaches 18%
Simulations suggest an AXIS‑like mission could boost photon counts by ~17×

jwst_massive_cosmic_structure.headline: James Webb Uncovers Ancient Galaxy Cluster XLSSC 122 Defying Cosmic Growth Models
jwst_massive_cosmic_structure.summary: NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has detected the distant XLSSC 122 cluster, revealing an unexpectedly dense dark‑matter core that challenges standard cosmology.
highlights: XLSSC 122 lies 10.4 billion light‑years away and shows strong gravitational lensing
The cluster’s central mass concentration exceeds predictions for its early‑universe age
Intracluster light traces dark‑matter distribution, offering a new mapping tool

dna_recording_embryo_development.headline: DNA Typewriter Maps Mouse Embryo Development From First Two Cells to Organs
dna_recording_embryo_development.summary: Scientists used a DNA recording system to trace mouse embryogenesis for 13.5 days, revealing staggered cell‑type commitments and lineage imbalances.
highlights: DNA Typewriter recorded every cell division in a fertilized mouse egg for 13.5 days
The two founder cells produced similar mixes of cell types despite unequal descendant numbers
Blood and retina lineages committed early, while skin epidermis remained flexible longer

ocean_circulation_amoc_failure.headline: AMOC May Persist for Centuries Even After NADW Collapse, Study Finds
ocean_circulation_amoc_failure.summary: Using CESM2 and an idealized reduced‑gravity model, researchers show that cross‑hemispheric overturning can continue for centuries despite a complete shutdown of NADW formation.
highlights: CESM2 simulation with quadrupled CO₂ shows full NADW shutdown but only gradual slowdown of overturning
Reduced‑gravity model attributes sustained circulation to deepening of density layers
A clockwise overturning emerges in the Indo‑Pacific, altering heat and nutrient distribution
Ventilation age in the deep Atlantic is projected to increase substantially

early_universe_faint_glow_dark_energy.headline: CHIME Detects Faint Hydrogen Glow to Probe Dark Energy
early_universe_faint_glow_dark_energy.summary: Using CHIME’s new autonomous hydrogen mapping, scientists have measured a 2% neutral hydrogen signal from 5 billion years ago, opening a cheaper path to study dark energy.
highlights: CHIME captured the faint radio glow of hydrogen from 5 billion years after the Big Bang
The signal shows roughly 2% of hydrogen was neutral at that epoch
The instrument can now map hydrogen without relying on costly galaxy‑survey cross‑correlations

gluon_string_ion_sim.headline: Trapped Ions Simulate Gluon String Breaking, Challenging Classic Theory
gluon_string_ion_sim.summary: Researchers at Duke University used a trapped‑ion quantum computer to model gluon string breaking, confirming earlier results and suggesting tweaks to longstanding theory.
highlights: The experiment employed domain walls in a chain of trapped ions to represent quark‑antiquark pairs.
An external magnetic field triggered the creation of additional domain walls, mimicking particle production.
Results align with prior simulations on superconducting qubits (Google Sycamore) and neutral‑atom arrays (QuEra).
Findings indicate string breaking initiates at edges, contrary to the original Schwinger picture.

quantum_energy_ladder_observation.headline: Physicists Observe Predicted ‘Energy Ladder’ at Quantum Critical Points
quantum_energy_ladder_observation.summary: An international Caltech team used a laser‑trapped strontium atom quantum simulator to experimentally reveal the long‑theorized energy ladder at Ising and tricritical quantum tipping points.
highlights: Energy levels appeared as discrete “rungs” matching conformal field theory predictions.
Experiments employed up to 35 strontium atoms excited to Rydberg states.
Both the Ising and tricritical points showed universal spectra after size rescaling.
Measurements were published in Nature after 40 years of theoretical anticipation.

tiny_genome_microbe_discovery.headline: Tiny Archaea Sukunaarchaeum mirabile Sets Record with 238 kb Genome
tiny_genome_microbe_discovery.summary: A newly described microbe living inside Japanese plankton possesses a 238 kb genome, challenging definitions of life by approaching the minimal genetic requirements for independent replication.
highlights: Sukunaarchaeum mirabile was discovered inside the plankton Citharistes regius off Shimoda, Japan
Its genome of 238 kilobase pairs is the smallest known for any archaeon
The organism lacks most metabolic genes yet retains DNA‑replication and protein‑production machinery
Researchers propose it may be a parasitic archaeon, only the second of its kind recorded

dinosaurs_pole_shift.headline: True Polar Wander Shifted Earth’s Poles Up to 0.6° per Million Years During Dinosaur Era
dinosaurs_pole_shift.summary: New research shows Earth’s crust moved faster than thought, causing rapid pole shifts that altered climate and sea levels in the Jurassic and Cretaceous.
highlights: Four true‑polar‑wander events identified between 190‑20 million years ago
Sea‑level changes displayed a quadrupolar pattern across hemispheres
Shifts reached up to 0.6° per million years, faster than plate tectonics

juno_magnetodisk_rippling.headline: Juno Data Shows Jupiter’s Magnetodisk Ripples Like a Wave
juno_magnetodisk_rippling.summary: New analysis of Juno measurements reveals Jupiter’s magnetodisk repeatedly warps into wave‑like ripples during active reconnection events, challenging prior smooth‑disk models.
highlights: Juno crossed the current sheet multiple times per rotation, detecting repeated magnetic signatures and energetic particle bursts
The rippling structure spans roughly 100° of longitude and persists from several minutes to over an hour
These findings suggest the magnetodisk may influence the acceleration and transport of Io’s volcanic particles

planet_320_ly_away_chemical_similarity.headline: Ultra‑Hot Jupiter WASP‑189b Mirrors Host Star’s Magnesium‑Silicon Ratio
planet_320_ly_away_chemical_similarity.summary: Astronomers using Gemini South’s IGRINS spectrograph measured magnesium and silicon in WASP‑189b, finding a ratio identical to its star and confirming a key planet‑formation assumption.
highlights: First simultaneous detection of magnesium and silicon in an exoplanet atmosphere
Mg/Si ratio on WASP‑189b matches that of its host star
Observations made with high‑resolution IGRINS on Gemini South in Chile
Study published in Nature Communications (2026) and based on peer‑reviewed data

physicists_outran_quantum_tornadoes_to_p.headline: Physicists Outrun Quantum Vortices to Probe Superconductor Depairing Limit
physicists_outran_quantum_tornadoes_to_p.summary: Using 300‑femtosecond laser pulses, researchers at the Max Planck Institute pushed NbN and YBCO beyond their vortex‑driven limits to reveal intrinsic depairing thresholds.
highlights: Optical‑electric circuit generated picosecond current pulses that outran vortex dynamics by orders of magnitude
NbN (s‑wave) retained superconductivity until a sharp depairing threshold, while YBCO (d‑wave) showed gradual weakening
The method directly accessed gap symmetry, a property inaccessible to conventional DC transport

ai_reveals_chemical_shortcut_co2_fuel.headline: AI uncovers hidden 9,389‑reaction pathway boosting CO₂‑to‑methanol conversion
ai_reveals_chemical_shortcut_co2_fuel.summary: Researchers at Indian Institute of Science used AI to expand a copper catalyst network to 9,389 reactions, revealing a hydrogen pathway that raises CO₂ conversion by about 40‑fold.
highlights: AI‑driven model grew from 152 to 9,389 reactions on a copper catalyst
Expanded network correctly predicts methanol and CO as major products
Hydrogen can transfer as intact H₂, challenging traditional mechanistic views

turning_disorder_into_resource_wave_cont.headline: Disorder Engineered Acoustic Waveguide Achieves Non‑Abelian Braiding
turning_disorder_into_resource_wave_cont.summary: Researchers used the generalized Wigner‑Smith operator to arrange eighty metallic cylinders, enabling near‑perfect transmission and non‑Abelian braiding of acoustic modes.
highlights: Designed a scattering medium that performs target unitary transformations while preserving transmission
Demonstrated non‑Abelian braiding of waveguide modes in a compact acoustic waveguide only a few wavelengths thick
Showed that complex media can be programmed for diverse wave‑based information processing

ghostly_galaxies_dark_matter.headline: Ghostly Galaxies Lacking Dark Matter Challenge Modified‑Gravity Theories
ghostly_galaxies_dark_matter.summary: Three ultra‑diffuse galaxies—DF2, DF4 and DF9—appear to contain almost no dark matter, providing fresh evidence that dark matter is a real substance rather than a tweak to gravity.
highlights: DF2, DF4 and DF9 each show mass‑to‑light ratios consistent with ordinary matter alone
A June 2026 paper in The Astrophysical Journal proposes a head‑on collision that stripped dark matter from the progenitor galaxies
The findings undermine modified‑gravity models such as MOND and bolster the particle‑dark‑matter paradigm

moon_two_faces_solution.headline: Earth’s Gravity May Have Driven Moon’s Two‑Face Asymmetry, New Study Shows
moon_two_faces_solution.summary: Analysis of Chang'e‑6 far‑side rocks reveals uniform mantle composition but a magnesium‑rich crust, supporting a heat‑driven magma circulation model.
highlights: Chang'e‑6 returned far‑side anorthosite, Mg‑suite and basalt samples for the first time
Chemical signatures show mantle cumulates are similar on both hemispheres, while crustal rocks differ in Mg# and Th/Sm ratios
Researchers propose Earth’s tidal heating created horizontal magma flow, thickening the far‑side crust and concentrating KREEP
The peer‑reviewed paper appears in National Science Review (2026)

zombie_cells_protein_discovery.headline: Blocking PD‑L2 Halts Zombie Cell Build‑Up, Boosts Metabolism in Mice
zombie_cells_protein_discovery.summary: Researchers at Cedars‑Sinai found that inhibiting the protein PD‑L2 clears senescent cells, reducing inflammation and improving glucose handling and strength in aged mice.
highlights: PD‑L2 expression rises in senescent human cells and with age in tissues
Genetic deletion or antibody blockade of PD‑L2 cuts senescent cell accumulation in mice
Mice with reduced PD‑L2 show better blood‑sugar regulation and increased grip strength

hypernova_non_existence.headline: Study Shows Hypernova Explosions May Never Have Occurred
hypernova_non_existence.summary: New models suggest that irregular supernovae, not hypernovae, can explain the unusual chemical signatures of halo stars, challenging the need for ultra‑energetic explosions.
highlights: Researchers at University College London modeled asymmetric supernova ejecta and reproduced the odd element mixes of four
Analysis of a Milky Way halo red giant revealed heavy elements like silver and uranium without neutron‑star‑merger signatures.
The findings, published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, argue that ordinary supernovae suffice to form

nepal_flood_seismic_analysis.headline: Seismic Study Pinpoints Timing of Nepal’s Deadly August Flood
nepal_flood_seismic_analysis.summary: Researchers used Nepal and Chinese seismometers to time the August 26 landslide at 8:37 a.m., revealing and possible precursor slide‑quakes.
highlights: The main mass movement began at 8:37 a.m. Nepal time, as determined from regional seismic data.
A magnitude‑2.5 event occurred 17 minutes before the collapse, but its role remains uncertain.
More than 60 small seismic events were recorded in the two weeks preceding the disaster, suggesting slide‑quake activity.
The collapse generated seismic amplitudes larger than the 2025 Tracy Arm landslide in Alaska.

2fle_catalog.headline: Second Catalog Reveals 450 Low‑Energy Gamma‑Ray Sources from Fermi‑LAT
2fle_catalog.summary: Using 14 years of Fermi‑LAT data, the 2FLE catalog lists 450 sources between 20 MeV and 200 MeV, highlighting dozens of new extragalactic and Galactic emitters.
highlights: 450 sources detected with TS>25 and median flux 1.9×10⁻¹¹ erg cm⁻² s⁻¹
377 sources associated with known counterparts, dominated by flat‑spectrum radio quasars (FSRQ)
60 newly discovered gamma‑ray sources, 51 at high latitudes, 38 exceeding 10σ significance
45 sources are TeV emitters and 6 coincide with 1LHAASO detections

act_dr6_alp_birefringence.headline: ACT Sets Tight New Limits on Axion‑Photon Coupling from Cosmic Birefringence
act_dr6_alp_birefringence.summary: Using five years of ACT polarization data, researchers find no time‑varying birefringence, tightening the axion‑photon coupling bound for ultra‑light dark‑matter candidates.
highlights: Analyzed over 10,000 time‑sliced polarization maps from 2017‑2022
Probed ALP masses from 2.5×10⁻²³ eV to 4.8×10⁻²⁰ eV
Set a 95% upper limit g_{φγ}<1.1×10⁻¹¹ GeV⁻¹ (m_φ/10⁻²¹ eV)
Achieved the strongest stochastic‑field CMB bounds to date

arxiv_2610_19318v1.headline: JWST Maps Cosmic Star Formation from Today to Reionization Using Hydrogen Lines
arxiv_2610_19318v1.summary: A combined JWST/NIRCam slitless survey of COSMOS and GOODS‑N traces dust‑corrected hydrogen recombination lines in 9,146 galaxies, revealing star‑formation trends from $z\sim0$ to 9.
highlights: 9146 galaxies observed across $0.33\,\mathrm{deg}^2$ in COSMOS and $60.9\,\mathrm{arcmin}^2$ in GOODS‑N
Line‑flux limits reach $3.2\times10^{-18}$ and $1.04\times10^{-18}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}}$ for the two fields
Six hydrogen lines (Brα, Brβ, Paα, Paβ, Hα, Hβ) converted to equivalent Hα luminosities
Schechter fits show characteristic Hα luminosity rising toward cosmic noon

arxiv_2610_19926v1.headline: JWST Dormant Galaxies at z>3 Found Gas‑Poor, Likely Heading Toward Death
arxiv_2610_19926v1.summary: A study using ALMA archival data shows that JWST‑identified dormant galaxies at z>3 have molecular gas fractions far below main‑sequence expectations, indicating rapid quenching.
highlights: Dormant galaxies at z>3 display SFR10Myr lower than SFR100Myr, signaling a recent star‑formation drop
ALMA [CII]158µm and CO limits reveal gas fractions 0.3‑2 dex beneath main‑sequence levels
Gas fractions of dormant and quiescent samples are statistically indistinguishable
The sample spans COSMOS, UDS, and GOODS‑South fields with log(Mstar/Msun)>9.5

xray_superflares_protoplanetary_disks.headline: Chandra‑JWST Study Links Moderate X‑Ray Superflares to Disk Atmosphere Changes
xray_superflares_protoplanetary_disks.summary: Coordinated Chandra and JWST/NIRSpec observations of Orion Nebula stars reveal that moderate X‑ray superflares subtly alter infrared spectral features of protoplanetary disks.
highlights: Ten flare stars and twelve control stars were observed across six Chandra/ACIS-I and three JWST/NIRSpec epochs.
Variable narrow infrared features decrease with distance from the O star Theta1 Ori C, suggesting external irradiation effects.
HI Br‑alpha shows stronger variability and unique absorption‑core profiles in flare stars, indicating magnetospheric accretion
The CO fundamental band shows no flare‑related changes, matching thermochemical model predictions for moderate superflares.

2610_19881v1.headline: JWST MIRI‑MRS Reveals Distinct PAH Populations in Orion Bar
2610_19881v1.summary: Using blind signal separation, researchers extracted two mid‑infrared template spectra from JWST observations, distinguishing UV‑exposed and shielded PAH groups distinct.
highlights: Two template spectra named AIBirrad and AIBshield were derived via non‑negative matrix factorization
AIBirrad traces large, compact ionized PAHs strongly irradiated by UV radiation
AIBshield traces small, asymmetric neutral PAHs with aliphatic side groups in more protected regions
The study utilizes data from the PDRs4All program’s JWST MIRI‑MRS observations of the Orion Bar

2610_18975v1.headline: Modulated Phase Transition Could Seed Cosmic Curvature and GW Anisotropies
2610_18975v1.summary: A post‑inflationary first‑order phase transition, modulated by a light spectator field, may generate the observed large‑scale curvature perturbations and detectable GW anisotropies.
highlights: The mechanism reproduces the observed amplitude of curvature perturbations while predicting a loud stochastic GW background
Intrinsic GW anisotropies are strongly enhanced, falling within the sensitivity of space‑based detectors such as LISA, Taiji
The model yields a local primordial non‑Gaussianity signal potentially observable by upcoming large‑scale‑structure surveys

2610_18964v1.headline: Kerr Black Hole Spin Boosts EMRI Rates by Up to 2.5‑Fold
2610_18964v1.summary: New Monte Carlo simulations incorporating inclination diffusion show that Kerr spin can increase detectable EMRI events by roughly 2.5 times compared to non‑spinning models.
highlights: Inclination diffusion allows prograde orbits to become retrograde, altering EMRI‑to‑plunge outcomes.
Simulations predict a ~2.5‑fold rise in EMRI detections for rapidly spinning massive black holes.
Even without spin, relativistic Kerr geodesics raise EMRI counts by a similar factor.
The resulting inclination distribution shows a strong prograde bias, aiding future EMRI identification.

ilmt_transient_discovery_2026.headline: Indian ILMT discovers supernova candidates, DOT provides spectroscopic confirmation
ilmt_transient_discovery_2026.summary: The 4‑m International Liquid Mirror Telescope (ILMT) identified several photometric transients, which were classified as supernovae through follow‑up spectroscopy with the 3.6‑m Devasthal Optical Telescope (DOT).
highlights: ILMT continuously surveys a 22.3′ × 22.3′ zenith strip, enabling nightly transient detection
PyLMT pipeline uses optimized image subtraction and CNN classification to flag candidates
DOT spectra confirmed the supernova nature of the selected transients
Combined ILMT light curves with ZTF data improve photometric characterization

2610_19009v1.headline: Euclid Finds First L‑type Substellar Object Near Embedded Cluster NGC 2023
2610_19009v1.summary: A young L3 dwarf, J054158.70‑021031.4, was spectroscopically confirmed by Euclid near NGC 2023, with a mass at the planetary‑mass boundary.
highlights: Spectral type L3 with Av = 3 mag reddening
Optical magnitude ≈ 24.5 in Euclid band
Distance estimated at 403 pc, placing it near the planetary‑mass limit
Proper motion aligns with nearby cluster NGC 2024

brain_implants_voice.headline: Brain Implants Restore Voice for ALS Patient Casey Harrell
brain_implants_voice.summary: A brain‑computer interface implanted in Casey Harrell’s speech motor cortex has enabled him to speak again after ALS robbed his natural voice.
highlights: Implanted four electrode grids on the left precentral gyrus in 2023
Harrell has generated nearly 2 million words using the system, reported in Nature Medicine
The decoder initially used a 50‑word vocabulary, later expanded to over 125,000 words

magnetic_fossils_deep_ocean_oxygen.headline: Magnetofossils Reveal Absolute Deep‑Ocean Oxygen Levels Past
magnetic_fossils_deep_ocean_oxygen.summary: Researchers linked nanoscopic magnetic fossils to present‑day oxygen concentrations, creating an equation to estimate absolute oxygen levels in ancient deep‑sea environments.
highlights: Analyzed over 200 modern ocean sediment samples from global basins
Documented shapes of more than 4,500 magnetite grains using a transmission electron microscope
Found that low‑oxygen waters host more bullet‑shaped magnetite, while high‑oxygen waters favor tiny cubic crystals

engineered_multi_resistance_fungal_defen.headline: Engineered Plant Immune Receptors Offer New Defense Against Blast Fungus
engineered_multi_resistance_fungal_defen.summary: Scientists engineered tandem kinase receptors to recognize multiple blast fungus effectors, paving way for durable resistance in rice, wheat and barley.
highlights: Modified TKP immune receptors now bind two distinct effectors from Magnaporthe oryzae
Structural analysis revealed HMA domains act as bait for fungal attack molecules
Dual‑specificity receptors could be stacked with NLRs for layered crop immunity

2610_18998v1.headline: JWST Reveals Convective‑Transition Gap in Globular Cluster 47 Tucanae
2610_18998v1.summary: Deep JWST imaging of 47 Tucanae uncovers a narrow convective‑transition gap along the lower main sequence, confirmed by stellar luminosity function analysis.
highlights: The gap appears as a sharp dip followed by a sudden rise in star counts in two independent colour‑magnitude diagrams.
Empirical likelihood modelling shows the feature is statistically significant beyond random fluctuations.
Additional JWST passbands reproduce the discontinuity, strengthening evidence for a genuine stellar structure.

brain_activity_under_anesthesia.headline: Anesthetized Brain Still Analyzes Language and Predicts Words, Study Finds
brain_activity_under_anesthesia.summary: Even under full general anesthesia, patients' hippocampi processed word categories and forecast upcoming words, revealing sophisticated unconscious neural activity.
highlights: Neuropixels probes recorded activity from hundreds of hippocampal neurons during anesthesia.
Neurons distinguished unexpected tones and showed plasticity despite lack of conscious awareness.
Distinct patterns encoded nouns, verbs, adjectives and predicted next words in spoken stories.
Findings published in Nature (2026) challenge assumptions about consciousness and may inform brain‑computer interfaces.

chemical_starter_kit_life.headline: ALMA Finds Deuterium‑Rich Methanol and Masers in Young Star Disks
chemical_starter_kit_life.summary: Using ALMA, the COMPASS survey detected deuterium‑enriched methanol and widespread maser emission in the planet‑forming disks of eleven low‑mass protostars.
highlights: Methanol (CH3OH) was found with deuterium in the disk of IRAS 4A2, a protostar in the Perseus Molecular Cloud.
Methanol maser emission was detected around more than half of the surveyed protostars, the first such observation in low‑mass
The study surveyed eleven nearby low‑mass protostars, revealing variations in oxygen‑ and nitrogen‑bearing molecules across the
Results were published in seven papers in the October 2026 issue of Astronomy & Astrophysics.

melting_permafrost_arctic_rivers.headline: Melting Permafrost Drives Acid Rock Drainage in Arctic Rivers
melting_permafrost_arctic_rivers.summary: Long‑term monitoring shows sulphate and zinc spikes in Brooks Range streams after the unusually warm 2019 winter, linked to oxidative weathering of thawed permafrost sulfides.
highlights: Sulphate concentrations rose sharply in rivers draining the Brooks Range
Zinc levels increased concurrently, indicating mobilization of sulfide minerals
The 2019 winter warmth triggered rapid permafrost thaw and exposure of acid‑producing rocks
Similar chemical shifts have been reported in Yukon watersheds, suggesting a broader regional impact

2610_20948v1.headline: JWST Links ULX Ho II X‑1 to Highly Ionized Nebula in Holmberg II
2610_20948v1.summary: JWST IFU spectroscopy resolves a 15‑25 pc nebula around ULX Ho II X‑1, detecting [Ne V] and [Ne VI] and revealing anisotropic ionization linked to radio jets.
highlights: First detection of [Ne V] and [Ne VI] emission from the ULX nebula.
Highest‑ionization lines originate from compact regions offset toward known radio knots.
Emission lines are narrow, indicating quiescent gas and ruling out shock‑driven ionization.
Ionization extends over ~100 pc, showing the ULX’s black hole powers extreme nebular excitation.

desi_dr1_lrg2_model_independent.headline: DESI DR1 LRG2 Analysis Yields Model‑Independent Distance and Growth Measurements
